papers.title: TAC2: Timestamped Audio Captioning as composable functions
papers.abstract: Real-world audio applications require precise, queryable representations grounded in physical time. Yet modern Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) increasingly favor conversational generation, producing free-form descriptions that conflate acoustic perception with higher-level reasoning and lack precise temporal grounding. We introduce TAC2, a foundation model that casts timestamped audio captioning as composable functions to construct granular, speaker-attributed acoustic timelines directly from in-the-wild audio. To avoid prohibitively expensive manual annotation, we programmatically fuse complementary predictions from specialized weak teachers through time-registered IoU matching. We model the resulting multi-granularity schema of timestamped events, speaker turns, and fine-grained speech attributes using an Instruction-Input-Output (IIO) completion format, in which each task is a function of the audio, an instruction, and an optional input. A single call decodes the full description autonomously, while composing calls lets earlier outputs or external priors, such as a reference transcript, condition later ones. We further extend TAC2 with expressive speech attributes to obtain TAC2-S, using parameter-efficient specialists to elicit latent paralinguistic capabilities from the pre-trained backbone and distill them into a unified model. We validate the resulting representation in two complementary settings. Paired with frozen text-only LLMs, it yields strong spoken audio understanding across diverse reasoning backends, demonstrating the utility of decoupling fine-grained acoustic perception from downstream reasoning. Used as paired supervision for text-to-audio generation, it supports semantically and temporally grounded reconstruction, together with explicit zero-shot control over event timing, speaker attributes, and word-level emphasis.

papers.title: Audio-R1: Audio Reasoning through Reinforcement Learning on Self-Supervised Tasks
papers.abstract: Reasoning is increasingly important for large audio-language models (LALMs), yet remains relatively underexplored compared with text-only and vision-language models. We introduce Audio-R1, a reinforcement learning (RL) post-training framework that revisits audio self-supervised learning as a source of verifiable rewards for improving audio understanding and reasoning task performance. Audio-R1 uses answers automatically determined during the construction of self-supervised tasks to verify model responses and compute rewards. Experiments across multiple LALMs and diverse audio benchmarks show consistent performance gains, while ablations demonstrate the benefits of each self-supervised task and additional gains from joint training. While both supervised fine-tuning and Audio-R1 improve self-supervised task accuracy, Audio-R1 further improves performance on downstream tasks distinct from the training tasks. These results highlight the potential of RL post-training with self-supervised audio tasks to improve downstream performance and reasoning-trace quality.

papers.title: Does Notation Matter? MusicXML Tokenisation for Symbolic Music Generation and Understanding
papers.abstract: Symbolic music representations encode musical content at varying levels of completeness, from performance-oriented formats such as MIDI to fully notated scores such as MusicXML. Yet the impact of this representational richness on deep learning models remains poorly understood. While tokenisation has been extensively studied for MIDI, score-based formats have received considerably less attention, and MusicXML in particular remains largely unexplored despite being the de-facto standard for score interchange. In this paper, we introduce the first general-purpose tokenisation framework for MusicXML, and conduct a systematic empirical study to determine whether notational richness confers a measurable advantage for deep learning on symbolic music. We train 26 autoregressive and masked language models, comparing MusicXML tokenisation against MIDI and ABC-based representations, probing the effect of different tokenisation strategies within MusicXML, and testing whether music-grammar-aware tokenisation outperforms treating scores as plain text. We evaluate music understanding tasks using linear probing across composer classification, difficulty estimation, and accompaniment suggestion, and generative tasks using objective statistical metrics and a human pairwise preference study. Our results show that MusicXML-tokenised models outperform MIDI and text-based counterparts on understanding and generative tasks.

papers.title: S3-S2ST: Semantically Supervised Streaming Speech-to-Speech Translation
papers.abstract: Streaming speech-to-speech translation requires timely decisions about when partial input is sufficient for accurate translation. We present S3-S2ST, a model that learns to translate and speak from semantically aligned streaming supervision. By converting utterance-level speech pairs into incremental training examples, we teach a learned policy when to commit translations. Its adjustable threshold controls the quality--latency tradeoff on a fixed 640\,ms input grid. S3-S2ST delivers competitive English--Chinese translation on FLEURS and leads the evaluated streaming systems in translation quality on the internal 9-pair test set. On RealSI, adapting the threshold to buffered speech further improves quality over a low fixed threshold with little change in first-audio latency. We plan to release the model and code.

papers.title: Uni-Stream: A Unified Streaming Speech Language Model for Speech Synthesis and Recognition
papers.abstract: Unified streaming speech language models aim to support speech recognition and synthesis within a single model, enabling real-time human-computer interaction. However, jointly supporting these two directions of speech-text conversion while preserving task-specific performance remains challenging. We propose Uni-Stream, a unified streaming speech language model built on compact pretrained speech models. Uni-Stream processes interleaved text and speech in a streaming format and achieves performance comparable to task-specific models through two-stage training. We also develop a data annotation pipeline for streaming training and will publicly release the generated transcriptions and word-level timestamps. We further examine Uni-Stream's representations across tasks and modalities and find that speech and text residence in distinct latent feature space even when trained in a unified model architecture, while representations within each modality become more task-dependent in later layers.

papers.title: Do Audio LLMs HEAR Pain? Tracing Acoustic Evidence from Speech to Language Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) can process speech directly, but it remains unclear how well they use the non-lexical acoustic information that speech carries. We study this question through pain, using TAME-Pain, which contains pain-neutral Harvard sentences and spoken pain ratings recorded at different self-reported pain levels. We introduce HEAR, a four-stage diagnostic framework that traces pain-related information from the speech signal to the model's prediction, and apply it to seven closed-source and open-weight LALMs. On the Harvard sentences, where pain can only be inferred from the voice, all models perform at chance level, and same-speaker references or few-shot examples improve balanced accuracy by no more than six points. On the spoken ratings, the same models reach 87.5-99.7% balanced accuracy. Layer-wise probing of open-weight LALMs shows that pain can be decoded from early audio representations (74.1% balanced accuracy for binary prediction and 45.0% for three-class severity), but that this information, along with most pain-associated acoustic cues, decreases in deeper layers. In an acoustic perception test, weaker models cannot distinguish even large changes in these cues, whereas stronger models can but still fail to infer pain. Finally, we recover pain-related acoustic cues and directly reinject them as structured text into the prompt, which improves pairwise pain prediction by up to 32 points. These results indicate that current LALMs encode paralinguistic information in early layers that is largely unavailable when the model produces its answer.

papers.title: In-Context Adapter Generation for Compositional Generalization in Large Audio Language Models
papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) have achieved strong performance on standard speech and audio understanding tasks, yet their ability to systematically generalize to novel task compositions remains underexplored. Taking a meta-learning view, we extend Text-to-LoRA (T2L) to LALMs, generating instruction-conditioned LoRA adapters with a Transformer hypernetwork rather than learning a single fixed adapter shared across instructions. To exploit fine-grained task information, we introduce in-context adapter generation (ICAG), a token-level hypernetwork architecture; we call the resulting method T2L-ICAG. We evaluate this approach on two representative LALMs using SIFT-50M for supervised fine-tuning and construct a controlled compositional evaluation suite covering five task classes. Across two LALM backbones, T2L-ICAG consistently improves over static LoRA and also the global embedding-based T2L baseline. Coverage and capacity analyses further show that these gains are larger on structurally out-of-domain tasks and cannot be explained by parameter count alone. These results suggest that generating task-specific adapters from instructions is a promising direction for improving compositional generalization of LALMs.

papers.title: Melody Guidance for Audio Diffusion Models Without Retraining
papers.abstract: Controlling melody in audio generation normally requires training a conditional generative model on audio paired with pitch curves or MIDI notes. We instead guide an existing unconditional diffusion model, originally trained without melody inputs, to follow a target melody without retraining or modifying it. During inference, a differentiable pitch detector steers the sampled audio toward the desired pitches, while the diffusion model keeps it close to the distribution of realistic audio learned during training. Our main contribution is a sampling method that balances these two directions, providing melody control while preserving audio quality. To improve stability, we initialize sampling with a simple synthesized version of the target melody rather than pure noise. Experiments on piano, guitar, and singing voice show melody accuracy comparable to conditional models trained specifically for melody control. Our method therefore adds melody control to existing audio diffusion models without requiring paired melody data or task-specific retraining.

papers.title: Reading-Level Verification of Kanji Words in Japanese Financial Speech Synthesis
papers.abstract: Few-shot voice cloning makes it cheap to produce daily Japanese financial commentary with several synthetic speakers, but kanji words with more than one reading, such as the word for "market" (shijo vs. ichiba) or "overall trend" (taisei vs. oze), are still misread. A common quality gate transcribes each synthesized sentence with automatic speech recognition (ASR), converts both the input and the transcript to kana, and regenerates on mismatch. We show that this gate is unreliable in both directions: when the audio contains a misreading, the ASR language model frequently writes the expected kanji back, hiding the error, and when the audio is correct, ordinary recognition errors trigger needless regeneration. We propose a reading-level check that scores the expected reading and its confusable alternatives with a connectionist temporal classification (CTC) hiragana recognizer and flags a word when an alternative explains the audio better. On 540 utterances from three voice-cloned production voices covering 30 financial terms, with misreadings injected under controlled conditions, the transcript-based gate detected 78.9% of misreadings at a 44.4% false-alarm rate, whereas the proposed check detected 91.7% at 5.0% (AUC 0.990). On natural kanji input, it caught a front-end error that the transcript-based gate missed for one voice, and reduced regeneration requests from 38.9% to 6.1% of sentences.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Generative Models for Music Audio
papers.abstract: Music audio generation spans instrumental clips, full songs with vocals, edits of existing recordings, and systems that play alongside a musician in real time. This monograph explains the methods behind these systems for readers familiar with neural-network training who are new to music generation. It introduces neural audio codecs and autoencoders, autoregressive and masked token models, diffusion and flow matching, sampling acceleration, and preference optimization in a shared notation. Worked examples connect training objectives and sampling procedures to published systems. The application sections relate the musical requirements of instrumental generation, songs, editing, and live performance to model design. Comparison tables record representations, methods, inputs, tasks, and release information documented in papers and official sources. Symbolic composition, speech, and sound effects are included where they connect to music audio. We explain how to interpret automatic metrics and learned judges, design and report listening tests, and assess evidence about data provenance, memorization, attribution, and output detection. Selected legal decisions and disputes illustrate the implications for training and release. The reviewed systems combine established generative paradigms with new representations, planning stages, and post-training procedures. Differences in data, scale, and evaluation limit what cross-system comparisons can establish about the sources of reported gains.

papers.title: AudioRSI: Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has made Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) better reasoners, but the reward that drives it still comes from outside the model: a final-answer check, a hand-crafted process score, or an external LLM judge that stays fixed while the policy improves. We show that an Audio LLM can supply this reward itself, and can do so recursively: each improved model becomes the critic that trains its successor, so the training signal improves along with the model. We introduce AudioRSI (Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners), a reinforcement learning framework in which a single model plays two roles: as an actor it generates reasoning paths, and as a critic it compares them pairwise, turning its own judgments into a process-level reward. The critic is periodically replaced by the current policy, which closes the recursive loop. Because the critic hears the same recording as the actor, it can reject reasoning that cites acoustic evidence the audio does not contain, rather than reward reasoning that merely sounds plausible. The recursion is what sustains progress: under a frozen external judge, out-of-distribution accuracy plateaus during training, while a critic refreshed from the improving policy keeps it rising. Across four out-of-distribution benchmarks, all disjoint from the AVQA training distribution, AudioRSI outperforms strong baselines including Audio Flamingo 3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on MMAU test-mini, ranks first on MMSU, achieves a clear lead on the challenging Multi-Audio split of MMAU-Pro, and leads the 7B open-source tier on MMAR among methods without external reward models. With no reward specifying how to reason, AudioRSI also develops structured reasoning behaviors (logical reasoning, perception-aware analysis, and reduced hallucination), corroborated by an external LLM-as-Judge evaluation and a keyword-based behavior analysis.

papers.title: MusicTwins: Training Audio-Language Models to Listen like Their Persona
papers.abstract: People differ in how they perceive music, what associations they make with it, what they like about it, and how they respond to it. Computational models intended to simulate people in environments that include music should account for these differences. Although LLMs have been shown to reproduce aspects of human behavior, whether audio-language models (ALMs) can reproduce a specific person's responses to textual and musical stimuli remains underexplored. We introduce MusicTwins, a framework that combines persona summaries, personal memory, and post-training to generate person-specific responses. We construct persona representations from human writings, capturing background, views, personality, writing style, and a musical profile, and post-train Audio Flamingo Next through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Evaluation on ten held-out personas shows notable improvements for Audio Flamingo Next in persona fidelity, including personality, writing style, and responses to music, supporting MusicTwins as a foundation for training audio-language models to listen like their persona.

papers.title: Concentrated Causal Influence, Distributed Diagnostic Information: Cognitive Impairment Decisions in Large Audio-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) can assess cognitive impairment (CI) from speech, yet their answers reveal neither which internal components control the decision nor how much CI information is accessible in their representations. We investigate both questions through CI-contrast neurons (CICNs), selected by class-contrastive activation frequency in decoder MLPs. Across eight open LALMs and two corpora (Pitt and PROCESS-2), we causally test CICNs against size- and layer-matched random masks and activity-matched controls. In three of the five models that meet our eligibility criteria, ablation of small CICN sets causes large, class-directed prediction shifts; speech-identified masks also control transcript-only decisions, and three of four primary Pitt masks retain specificity on PROCESS-2. Position-restricted interventions locate the influence before the final answer position, most strongly after the speech or transcript evidence under letter-labeled options, largely as a decision-direction shift. Beyond causal localization, supervised linear readouts of frozen CICN activations achieve 0.92--0.97 AUC within Pitt, versus 0.67--0.84 for the models' direct answers. Matched random and all-neuron readouts reach comparable performance; top-ranked CICNs show only an exploratory advantage at very small unit budgets. These results distinguish concentrated causal control over output decisions from broadly distributed diagnostic information for CI detection in LALMs.

papers.title: Pronunciation-Supervised Text-to-Speech for Irish (Gaeilge)
papers.abstract: Speech technology for Irish must be built from very little transcribed speech, yet the language's pronunciation is thoroughly documented in dictionaries and dialect descriptions. We ask whether that documentation can supervise the adaptation of a large pretrained text-to-speech model to a language it was never trained on. We adapt Qwen3-TTS to Irish using 12.8 hours of crowdsourced Common Voice speech, correcting two defects in the vendor fine-tuning script that training loss does not reveal (Appendix A), and reach character error rate (CER) 0.225 on held-out cross-corpus text, against 0.397 for an exhaustively tuned from-scratch system and 0.437 for zero-shot cloning. We then compile the Wiktionary pronunciation record into a lexicon and a phoneme critic, and use that critic as the verifier in one round of rejection fine-tuning: CER 0.159 cross-corpus and 0.067 in-domain, with the voice still anonymous across all 202 training speakers. The same critic explains why the voice cannot yet be steered to a minority dialect: 229 of 12,311 training clips lean Ulster against 8,451 Munster. Pronunciation documentation, converted into a verifier, is a practical lever for low-resource speech synthesis, and a way to measure what the available data cannot support.

papers.title: DRC-TTS: A Dual-Resolution Codec-Based Architecture for Lexicon-Free Malay Speech Synthesis
papers.abstract: Modern discrete neural audio codecs facilitate speech synthesis by replacing continuous acoustic representations with low-frame-rate discrete token sequences. For Malay speech synthesis, character-level input reduces reliance on pronunciation lexicons. However, combining character-level inputs with low-frame-rate discrete codecs introduces a temporal alignment challenge. When predicted character durations are quantized into frame counts at 12.5 Hz, durations shorter than one codec frame may be assigned zero frames. Consequently, the corresponding character representations may be lost during length regulation, potentially leading to pronunciation omissions. This study proposes DRC-TTS, a dual-resolution codec-based architecture for lexicon-free Malay speech synthesis. The model expands character representations at a temporal resolution of 50 Hz and subsequently downsamples them through strided convolution to 12.5 Hz for discrete codec-token prediction. Objective evaluations show that the proposed model reduces the character error rate (CER) from 27.11% for the baseline to 21.86%, an absolute reduction of 5.25 percentage points. The proposed model also achieves a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.30, compared with 4.12 for the baseline. These results suggest that the dual-resolution design may improve character-level alignment and perceived speech naturalness under the evaluated conditions.

papers.title: MixCards: Evaluating Structured Descriptions of Multi-Source Sound Scenes
papers.abstract: Audio captioning benchmarks typically evaluate a single unstructured free-text description of an audio scene, providing limited insight into how a model fails to understand polyphonic audio. A plausible caption may omit a source, or conflate multiple sources into one, or assign an attribute of one source to another, and conventional captioning evaluation cannot locate these errors. We introduce MixCardBench, a benchmark for structured captioning of polyphonic audio, which evaluates models in two stages: first, identifying and temporally localizing the sources in a scene, and second, generating a structured MixCard describing the semantic, temporal, and acoustic properties of each source. The benchmark contains 4884 ecologically plausible synthetic soundscapes with up to nine overlapping speech, music and sound effects sources built from high-quality recordings and source-level annotations, where each source has a reference MixCard. We evaluate six state-of-the-art large audio language models and find substantial limitations in current models, which struggle considerably with speech and sound effects timing and detection, with the strongest model reaching only around 60% mean card-field score. Performance varies significantly across attributes, exposing capability differences that are hidden by aggregate caption scores. We assess the quality and ecological validity of MixCardBench through human validation, distribution matching and a listening study, and show that human corrections have little effect on model rankings, and our synthesized soundscapes are closer to in-the-wild YouTube videos than source guided but otherwise random synthesis. The benchmark dataset and code are publicly available, and demo examples are at https://mixcards-anon.github.io/mixcards-demo/

papers.title: StreamSE: Neural Audio Codec-based Streaming Speech Enhancement for On-device Inference
papers.abstract: Recent generative speech enhancement (SE) models achieve high perceptual quality, but their non-causal processing and expensive computation make them difficult to use for streaming, on-device inference. We propose StreamSE, a 20M-parameter streaming SE model that operates in the latent space of a frozen pretrained neural audio codec. At each frame, StreamSE directly regresses a clean continuous latent from the noisy continuous latent while conditioning on its own predictions from previous frames. Enhancement therefore requires a single forward pass per frame and no iterative sampling or look-ahead. We further truncate the codec's residual vector quantizer (RVQ) to its coarse levels, halving the number of tokens per frame while improving robustness to reverberation. StreamSE is the only streaming generative model in our comparison, yet it matches or exceeds the perceptual quality of the offline generative baselines. Furthermore, the complete StreamSE pipeline runs in real time on a single smartphone CPU core. Our results show that continuous latent regression provides a practical route to generative SE under fully causal, on-device streaming constraints.

papers.title: Developing a Speech Language Model for Basque
papers.abstract: Although the recent development of LLMs has paved the way for multi-modal interaction, minority languages face difficulties keeping pace. This work presents the first open Speech Language Model for Basque, designed for low-latency, end-to-end spoken interaction. Based on the LLaMA-Omni architecture, the system integrates a Latxa model as its backbone, transferring its Basque capabilities to the spoken modality by fine-tuning several modules. To address data scarcity, the English VoiceAssistant-400K corpus was translated into Basque, and the audio was synthesized using a Basque TTS. Evaluation results confirm the system's viability, achieving 3.86/5 in content quality, a 9.94% WER for spoken intelligibility, and a 3.07 UTMOS for audio quality. This work demonstrates that advanced spoken interaction systems can be developed using modular architectures and synthetic data even in low-resource languages.

papers.title: From Speech Tokens to Stolen Voices: Attacker-Chosen-Text Speaker Impersonation via Representation Inversion
papers.abstract: Speech interaction systems have gradually evolved from traditional cascaded systems that use text as intermediate information to end-to-end speech language models that directly process speech representations. In some applications, the speech frontend runs on the user's device and sends speech representations to a remote server for inference, while the original audio remains local. However, these representations may still contain speaker identity information. If an attacker obtains them, it may use this information to imitate the user's voice, threatening their voice privacy. To investigate this risk, we propose \stia, a Speech Token Inversion Attack that generates speech with attacker-specified text in a victim's voice using a single short leaked representation, without access to the original audio or its transcript. Specifically, \stia converts discrete, continuous, or mixed speech representations into conditioning sequences and trains a conditional flow-matching speech generation model using pairs of different utterances from the same speaker in public speech datasets. The model combines speaker characteristics contained in the leaked representation with the specified text to generate speech in the victim's voice. Experiments show that, with a Moshi representation leak corresponding to 3 seconds of speech, \stia achieves an average CAM++ speaker cosine similarity of 0.78 and a target-text word error rate of 3.80\%. These results show that speech frontend representations reveal reusable speaker identity information and highlight the need to consider privacy risks when designing speech frontend representation methods.

papers.title: Beyond Utterance-Level Speaker Similarity: Perception-Aligned Segmental Evaluation of Accent in Speech Generation
papers.abstract: Utterance-level similarity ratings do not reveal where perceived accent differences occur in generated speech. We introduce a segmental evaluation protocol combining speaker and accent similarity ratings with subword annotations of perceived accent differences provided by listeners from target accent regions. Using newly collected recordings, 47 retained listeners evaluate 200 content-matched reference--candidate pairs spanning four Scottish and Australian voices, two zero-shot TTS systems, and an articulation-based voice conversion system. Subword annotations locate salient pronunciation differences and sometimes yield different system rankings from similarity ratings. Speaker and accent ratings remain strongly associated ($\rho = 0.71$), highlighting the value of examining local perceptual evidence beyond these scores. Evaluation of seven objective distances reveals weak correspondence with subword selections, with correlations reaching at most $\rho = 0.22$. We release code, data, and an interactive demo to support the development of perceptually grounded segmental accent evaluation.

papers.title: Spatial Audio Generation and Editing with Executable Plans and Self-Distilling Transfusion
papers.abstract: Spatial audio authoring coordinates source decisions with soundfield synthesis. For editing, plans specify what to change and retain, while reference audio supplies further acoustic detail. We present AMBIT, a unified framework for native First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) generation and editing with three connected contributions. First, a shared Transfusion backbone couples autoregressive planning with rectified-flow rendering through executable ScenePlans that specify source content, activity, and 3D trajectories. For editing, the plan describes the full target scene, including retained sources; contrastive features ground the requested change, while full reference latents supply residual acoustic detail for preservation. Second, an FOA-aware continuous VAE combines shared-decoder omnidirectional recovery, asymmetric grouped KL, and spatial covariance matching to preserve content and inter-channel structure. Third, joint Transfusion on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) refines planning on student-generated prefixes and rendering at sampling states reached under student plans, with target-conditioned teachers supervising both modes of the shared student. Evaluations across speech, music, and sound show improved generation content and spatial quality, acoustic fidelity during instruction-guided editing, and unedited-source preservation over the compared baselines. papers.title: Beyond Answer Changes: Matched Same-Class Controls for Local Audio Evidence
papers.abstract: For audio-language models, an answer change after a local sound-event edit can reflect a response to the event's class, sensitivity to waveform rewriting, or both. We compare matched same-class and different-class replacements of a queried event. Both use the same interval, level estimate, donor fitting, and crossfade, while the same-class replacement preserves the correct answer. Across 600 synthetic soundscapes and three models from two architecture families, different-class replacements produce 49.7 to 60.9 percentage points more answer changes than same-class replacements. Same-class accuracy remains within 5.2 percentage points of original accuracy. Among trials with correct original and same-class answers, soundscape-weighted selective accuracy for the inserted class is 73.7 to 81.9%, averaging eligible trials within each soundscape and then weighting eligible soundscapes equally. This protocol tests how model answers respond to local changes in event class.

papers.title: AI-Based Voice to Music Generation System
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and generative models has created new opportunities for automating creative processes, particularly in music composition and audio production. Traditional music creation often requires musical knowledge, instrument-playing skills, professional audio-editing tools, and considerable time. These requirements can make music production challenging for beginners and individuals without formal musical training. To address these challenges, this research proposes an AI-Based Voice-to-Music Generation System that enables users to create musical compositions through natural voice commands. The proposed system aims to integrate speech recognition, natural language processing, audio signal processing, and AI-based music generation into a unified framework. Users can provide voice commands through a microphone or upload audio recordings describing their musical preferences. The system processes the input using speech recognition techniques to convert speech into text. Natural Language Processing is then applied to identify relevant musical characteristics, including genre, mood, tempo, and instrument preferences. Based on the extracted information, an appropriate generative music model produces a musical composition corresponding to the user's instructions. The generated audio is subsequently processed and made available for playback, saving, and downloading through an interactive user interface. The effectiveness of the proposed system will be investigated through experiments evaluating speech recognition accuracy, musical command interpretation, music generation quality, processing time, and user satisfaction. papers.title: Understanding Everyday Communication Patterns, Stress, and Productivity in Hybrid Work through Egocentric Wearable Audio Sensing
papers.abstract: The hybrid work trend in the post-COVID period has transformed how people communicate while at work. However, there is a lack of quantitative understanding of how home and office environments shape communicative behavior and affective well-being. To study this, as a part of a larger study of the role of work environment on stress, we designed an egocentric wearable audio sensing system that captured interpersonal communication across both working locations. The system extracts real-time acoustic features on a wearable audio sensor and performs offline foreground speaker diarization to derive speaking load and activeness features. To improve diarization performance under low-dimensional feature constraints, we apply a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework that transfers knowledge from large-scale speech foundation models into a compact ResNet-based model, achieving consistent improvements in diarization performance over the baseline across three public egocentric speech datasets. In a four-month longitudinal deployment with 16 participants, our system revealed location-dependent differences in work communication patterns. Moreover, the mixed linear model analyses showed that office-based speaking load was significantly associated with higher self-reported stress and lower self-reported productivity, while speaking activeness during home-based work amplified both productivity and affective load in this cohort.

papers.title: SimPOTrans: Self-Adaptation for Offline-to-Simultaneous Speech Translation via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Simultaneous speech translation (SimulST) aims to translate ongoing speech with low latency while preserving translation quality. Recent studies have adopted large language models (LLMs) for SimulST and formulated it as a multi-turn dialogue task for efficient generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance. However, existing dialogue-style SimulST approaches typically rely on specialized training schemes to acquire simultaneous translation behavior, either using synthesized read/write trajectories, which may provide suboptimal training signals, or jointly optimizing translation quality and latency, whose competing objectives may cause optimization instability. In this paper, we introduce SimPOTrans, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that enables offline speech translation models to self-adapt to dialogue-style SimulST. Through a simple two-stage RL post-training pipeline, SimPOTrans rewards an offline model for exhibiting translation behaviors beneficial to simultaneous scenarios when given partial speech inputs, thereby enabling offline-to-simultaneous self-adaptation without synthesized read/write trajectories or explicit latency optimization. At inference time, SimPOTrans requires no external decision policy and enables flexible quality--latency control by simply adjusting the chunk size of speech input. Experiments on the ACL 60/60 and MCIF benchmarks across three language directions (En$\rightarrow$De, En$\rightarrow$Zh, and En$\rightarrow$Ja) demonstrate that SimPOTrans outperforms several strong baselines, achieving a superior quality--latency trade-off.

papers.title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
papers.abstract: Expanding multilingual ASR systems to new languages is challenging when adaptation must preserve previously supported languages without replaying source-language training data. We study this problem in connector-based Speech LLMs, where a trainable connector maps speech representations into a frozen large language model. We evaluate target-update construction and merging strategies for adapting the connector while preserving source-language performance. In single-target expansion, target-only fine-tuning and standard TIES merging learn new languages but cause severe source-language forgetting, while SSU-Wanda+TIES gives the best source-preserving trade-off. In multi-target expansion, update merging provides stable source retention, whereas recursive expansion can improve target adaptation under favorable orders but is highly order-sensitive. These results show that multilingual ASR expansion requires balancing target acquisition, source retention, and interactions among target-language updates.

papers.title: ImageTTS: Repurposing Pretrained Image Diffusion Transformers for Speech Synthesis
papers.abstract: Pretrained image-generation models have been successfully repurposed for various downstream visual tasks. Whether their learned representations and generative priors can transfer beyond vision to other modalities remains largely unresolved, particularly for speech synthesis, which requires linguistic fidelity and preservation of speaker identity from a short reference. We present ImageTTS, which repurposes FLUX.2 for speech synthesis by encoding pseudo-RGB log-mel spectrograms with its frozen image VAE and adapting only its pretrained Diffusion Transformer (DiT) using conditional latent flow matching. This formulation disentangles two forms of vision-to-speech transfer: representation transfer through the image VAE and generative-prior transfer through DiT initialization. The frozen image VAE largely preserves intelligibility and speaker identity with 0.99 STOI and 0.95 speaker similarity, while image-pretrained DiT initialization accelerates convergence and improves linguistic accuracy, reducing WER from 4.2\% to 2.7\% at 100k matched updates relative to random initialization. The same framework supports both zero-shot and instruction-guided TTS and, when scaled to 100K hours of speech data, achieves 1.12\% WER on Seed-TTS test-en and a Style-ACC of 0.66 on CapSpeech, outperforming speech-native baselines trained on comparable data across both tasks. These results suggest that pretrained image models can transfer beyond architectural reuse, supplying useful latent representations and generative priors for intelligible and controllable speech synthesis.

papers.title: ASR-Protected Fusion and Reference-Anchored Policy Optimization for Joint ASR and Word-Level Speech Anti-Spoofing
papers.abstract: Existing anti-spoofing systems report either an utterance-level score or a time-based spoof interval: the former cannot show which words are spoofed, while the latter does not directly match the transcript and must be post-aligned with words, so alignment errors can lead to wrong word-level labels. Standard ASR model outputs only text; spoof information in the audio is lost after recognition and is not passed with the transcript. Yet changing only a few words can change the meaning of a sentence, leaving downstream systems to use incorrect text without knowing which words are spoofed. We therefore treat partial anti-spoofing as tagged ASR: the model transcribes speech and marks spoofed words at the same time, directly linking spoof labels to output words. We adopt the audio LLM and use ASR-Protected Subspace Gated Fusion (APSGF) to fuse spoof cues with ASR features. Spoof cues are added only outside an ASR-protected subspace, so they do not disturb recognition features. After cross-entropy training, we fine-tune the model with Reference-Anchored Policy Optimization (RAPO). Since the SFT policy is already concentrated, multiple samples from the same input tend to receive similar rewards, resulting in weak group-wise advantages. RAPO instead generates a single sample with low sampling randomness and anchors its advantage to the reward of a reference model. This allows the model to reinforce responses that outperform the reference while suppressing those that underperform it. Experiments on five datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in jointly detecting spoofed words and preserving ASR accuracy. The code is publicly available.

papers.title: Probing the phon* representations of the Mimi codebooks
papers.abstract: Neural audio codecs are increasingly used to encode speech for integration with large language models. This paper investigates the phonetic representations in the first codebook (CB0) of the Mimi codec. ABX style evaluation is poorly suited to Mimi fixed 80 ms tokenization window, which often spans multiple phonemes; we instead use forced alignment, entropy analysis, and Phone-Normalized Mutual Information (PNMI). Using TIMIT speech (58/55 speakers, SA1/SA2), individual tokens are strongly associated with specific phonemes (PNMI = 0.84, above random), yet phonemes are realized by multiple competing tokens rather than a one-to-one mapping.

papers.title: SpeakerTurn: Target-Speaker Semantic Turn Detection in Multi-Speaker Environments
papers.abstract: Semantic completeness alone cannot determine when an assistant should respond in a multi-speaker environment: a completed utterance may belong to an interfering speaker, while the designated user is still speaking, acknowledging, or requesting time. We therefore study semantic turn inference conditioned on speaker identity. We propose SpeakerTurn, a framework that jointly predicts the target transcript and turn state from a speech mixture and an independent target-speaker reference. Built on CocktailASR-1, it links semantic decisions to the corresponding target content through joint supervision, distinguishing complete, incomplete, backchannel, wait, and target-absent states, with a separate interruption task. We also examine whether structured chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision improves decisions by representing speaker presence and semantic cues. On a synthetic multi-speaker test set, SpeakerTurn achieves five-state macro F1 of 0.811 and target-transcription character error rate (CER) of 4.20%, correctly resolving all ten reference-swapped interruption pairs. Joint-format transcription and native-interface recognition nevertheless behave differently, and CoT improves validation transcription without improving turn macro F1. These results show why target attribution, semantic turn discrimination, and recognition retention require separate assessment when adapting speech language models for speaker-conditioned interaction.

papers.title: SonoWorld4D: From One Video to a 4D Audio-Visual Scene via Diffusion Synchronization
papers.abstract: Recent progress in visual scene generation has extended beyond static 3D scenes toward the more challenging problem of generating dynamic 4D scenes from minimal input. However, sound, despite being intrinsically coupled with dynamic objects and events, remains largely unmodeled in prior work. We introduce Video-to-4DAVScene, a new task that turns a video into an explorable, time-varying 4D audio-visual scene, and present the SonoWorld4D framework for this task. Given a monocular video, our method generates a 360 static background, reconstructs explicit motion trajectories of dynamic, sound-emitting foreground objects, and synthesizes a physically-grounded sound field consistent across multiple sources through dual-space audio diffusion synchronization. The resulting 4D scene supports real-time novel-view visual and spatial audio rendering. Evaluation on real-world dynamic scenes and a user study demonstrates SonoWorld4D generates 4D audio-visual scenes with perceptually realistic, physically grounded spatial audio consistent with scene geometry and visual content.

papers.title: Partially Edited Audio: Generation, Defense, and Open Problems
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative audio models facilitate increasingly flexible and selective editing of linguistic content and paralinguistic, extralinguistic, and other attributes. This paradigm, named partially edited audio, differs from full audio generation as only portions of the real recording are edited. This technique can serve both beneficial and harmful applications. We therefore present a concise survey from both generation and defense perspectives, focusing on audio, as a contribution to the ICASSP 2027 special session entitled "Partially Edited Media: Perspectives from Synthesis and Defense." We first define partially edited audio and argue that what counts as ``fake'' or harmful is an application-dependent judgment, not a fixed property of the edit. We then survey audio editing by editing target, approaches, and evaluation, and then defense methods by detection, localization, diarization, and interpretability, summarizing representative benchmarks and toolkits. Finally, we discuss future directions and open problems.

papers.title: WiP: VishGuard-M: Toward Voice-Authenticity-Aware Vishing Detection on Mobile Devices
papers.abstract: Generative AI has intensified voice phishing (vishing) through real-time voice cloning and LLM-driven conversational adaptation. State-of-the-art on-device defenses such as MmVTD analyze only transcripts and on-screen behavior, with no mechanism to verify the acoustic stream's authenticity. We present VishGuard-M, a lightweight dual branch framework pairing local voice-authenticity verification with linguistic intent classification. A compact AASIST-L acoustic branch (85K parameters) detects synthetic voice artifacts, while an INT8-quantized Whisper-DistilBERT pipeline scores phishing intent. To avoid the confidence dilution of linear averaging, we propose a max-score fusion rule (sfused = max(sa, sn)) that alerts if either branch flags a threat. Evaluated on the ASVspoof 2019 LA benchmark, compact AASIST-L variant achieves a 1.52% Equal Error Rate (EER) matching within 0.09 points the accuracy of full 298K parameter AASIST architecture (1.43% EER) while operating at less than a third of its parameter footprint. Concurrently, the linguistic branch achieves a 0.966 F1-score on an SMS phishing intent proxy dataset. Both branches are validated independently; joint on-device deployment is ongoing work. VishGuard-M outlines a zero-server, privacy-preserving blueprint for multi-modal vishing mitigation on mobile devices.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 32nd Annual International Conference on Mobile Computing and Networking

papers.title: ConformalMOS: Uncertainty-Aware MOS Prediction with Conformal Intervals and Ordinal Modeling
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of human Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) is crucial for evaluating synthetic speech quality in text-to-speech (TTS) and voice conversion (VC). Most MOS predictors output only point estimates and ignore uncertainty, limiting reliability in model selection and deployment. We propose ConformalMOS, a framework that augments MOS prediction with conformal prediction to produce statistically valid prediction intervals with guaranteed coverage under exchangeability, alongside point estimates. During training, MOS labels are modeled in an ordinal-aware manner by converting one-hot targets into Gaussian-smoothed distributions, preserving score ordering. This improves uncertainty calibration, particularly when softmax confidence is overconfident on out-of-distribution speech. On BVCC datasets, ConformalMOS achieves competitive accuracy (MSE = 0.08) while delivering empirically validated coverage, enhancing reliability for real-world TTS and VC deployment.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Elder-Scam Defense: A Review of Detection Methods for Human- and AI-Generated Fraud and a Layered Protection Framework
papers.abstract: Scams targeting older adults increasingly combine social engineering with generative technology such as voice cloning, video deepfakes and text produced by large language models (LLMs). Adults aged 60 and over reported losses of USD 7.7 billion to the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center in 2025, 59% more than in 2024. This review, supported by a documented search of four databases (2019–2026), examines how such scams are structured, why older adults are susceptible, and how artificial intelligence (AI) can detect or mitigate them. Of 992 screened records, 60 studies met the eligibility criteria, and three more were identified through citation chasing. Most evaluations with older users measured knowledge, confidence or intentions after an educational intervention; where detection performance or real-world exposure was measured, results were mixed and often null. None of the included studies evaluated an AI-based scam-detection system with older users in a field setting, and the only study testing audio-deepfake detectors on older speakers found that detectors trained on standard benchmarks roughly doubled their error rate. We propose a six-layer conceptual framework, not yet validated, for engineering elder-scam protection as a socio-technical system, and identify age-diverse evaluation, field trials of real-time assistance, privacy preservation and trust calibration as the principal open challenges.

Ming-3.0-audio-flash

Hear clearly. Understand deeply. Act intelligently.

Ming-3.0-audio-flash is a native audio-language model from inclusionAI. It accepts audio together with text instructions and supports speech recognition, spoken question answering, audio understanding, audio reasoning, and optional synthesized-speech responses.
GitHub · 🤖 ModelScope · 🤗 Flash · 🤗 Tiny · 💻 Examples
## Model Summary | Property | Description | | --- | --- | | Developer | inclusionAI | | Model type | Native audio-language Mixture-of-Experts model | | Parameters | 126B total parameters, 6.5B activated per inference step | | Inputs | Audio and text instructions | | Outputs | Text, or text with optional synthesized speech | | Primary languages | Chinese and English, including varied accents and dialects | | License | MIT | ## Highlights - **Complex speech recognition:** Handles Chinese and English speech, dialects, accents, noisy environments, and multi-speaker recordings. - **Long-audio understanding:** Comprehends and analyzes long-form recordings. - **Multidimensional perception:** Understands speech, non-speech sounds, acoustic scenes, and music. - **Audio reasoning:** Answers questions and performs reasoning over audio content. - **Audio interaction:** Produces text responses and can optionally synthesize speech with built-in voices or a reference voice. ## Architecture Ming-3.0-audio-flash combines an audio encoder and projector with a Mixture-of-Experts language backbone. An optional Talker generates speech responses from the model's output.

## Quick Start with Transformers The model uses custom Transformers code. Review the repository code before enabling `trust_remote_code=True`. ```bash git clone https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash.git cd Ming-3.0-audio-flash python -m venv .venv-transformers source .venv-transformers/bin/activate pip install -r requirements-transformers.txt ``` ### Audio Understanding ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --prompt "Please answer the question in the audio." ``` ### Speech Recognition ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --task asr \ --max-new-tokens 256 \ --no-repeat-ngram-size 10 ``` The validated ASR prompt asks the model to identify the spoken language and place a tab between the language label and transcription. ### Direct Python Usage ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash" audio_path = "examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained( model_id, trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=False, ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", trust_remote_code=True, ).eval() messages = [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "audio", "audio": audio_path}, {"type": "text", "text": "Please answer the question in the audio."}, ], } ] inputs = processor(messages).to(model.device) inputs["audio_feats"] = inputs["audio_feats"].to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=512, do_sample=False, ) generated_ids = output_ids[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :] response = processor.decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True).strip() print(response) ``` ## Speech Output The Talker example supports built-in voices and reference-audio voice prompting: ```bash python examples/transformers_thinker_talker.py \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --audio examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --voice US_Stella \ --output output.wav ``` See the [voice guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/docs/voices.md) for available voice names and reference-audio usage. ## Serving ### vLLM-Omni ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash MING_OUTPUT_MODE=text ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The reference 128K serving profile uses tensor parallelism across four 80 GB H800 GPUs. Select the deployment YAML that matches text-only or Talker output. On particularly long audio inputs, the four-GPU profiles may OOM; in that case, switch to the corresponding eight-GPU fallback profile (`deploy/*_8gpu.yaml`), which sets `tensor_parallel_size: 8` across GPUs 0–7 (and the Talker reuses GPU 7). See the [deployment guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/README.md#vllm-omni) for details. For speech output, start the audio profile and select an IP or registered voice with the vLLM-Omni client's `--voice` option: ```bash MING_OUTPUT_MODE=audio ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" python examples/vllm_omni_audio_chat.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --audio-response \ --voice US_Stella \ --output-audio outputs/answer.wav ``` The client sends this selection as Chat Completions `audio.voice: {"id": "..."}`. vLLM-Omni uses the built-in IP voice `灵小柔` when no voice is specified. The model directory also provides `灵楷` and `US_James` as preset reference voices under `voice_presets/voice_audio/`, with their matching transcripts in `voice_presets/voice_prompts.json`. Both names are also available as built-in IP voices. ### SGLang ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash ./scripts/serve_sglang.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The validated SGLang profile uses four GPUs and provides text output. See the [SGLang example](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/examples/sglang_audio_chat.py) for client usage. ### SGLang-Omni [SGLang-Omni](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/) serves transcription, audio chat, and speech synthesis from one server. Serving uses two GPUs: `--thinker.tp_size 2` places the thinker on both visible devices, the audio encoder uses GPU 0, and speech synthesis uses GPU 1. ```bash CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 sgl-omni serve \ --model-path inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --thinker.tp_size 2 ``` The server exposes OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/transcriptions`, `/v1/audio/speech`, and `/v1/chat/completions` endpoints. See the [SGLang-Omni cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/ming3_audio.html) for client examples, including voice cloning with `ref_audio` and `ref_text`. ## Evaluation ### Speech Recognition

# MiniMax Music 3 **MiniMax Music 3** is a high-performance music generation model for creating complete songs up to **five minutes** long. Conditioned on lyrics and a detailed music description, it generates structurally coherent songs with expressive vocals, evolving arrangements, and stable long-form audio quality. MiniMax Music 3 combines an **8B Global LLM** for long-range musical structure, a **0.6B Local LLM** for frame-level acoustic detail, and a continuous hidden-state synthesis system based on **Flow Matching** and **Flow-VAE**. The model produces 32 kHz, 16-bit stereo WAV audio. ## Demo Explore music generation examples on the [MiniMax Music 3 Demo](https://minimax-ai.github.io/music3-demo/).

## Complete Songs with Long-Range Coherence MiniMax Music 3 natively supports full-song generation up to five minutes. The model maintains musical themes, rhythm, vocal identity, and arrangement progression across long sequences, enabling complete structures such as intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, instrumental break, and outro. ## Fine-Grained Music Control The model accepts two complementary inputs: - **Lyrics** define the words to be sung and may include explicit section tags such as `[Intro]`, `[Verse]`, `[Pre-Chorus]`, `[Chorus]`, `[Post-Chorus]`, `[Bridge]`, `[Instrumental]`, `[Solo]`, and `[Outro]`. - **Music description** defines the musical style, emotional progression, vocal performance, instrumentation, arrangement, and production profile. For precise control, we recommend using a Structured Caption with three sections: - **Global Metadata**: genre, subgenre, BPM, key, scale, emotional progression, listening scenario, and production profile. - **Vocal Details**: vocal gender, timbre, performance style, harmony, backing vocals, and vocal effects. - **Arrangement**: primary and secondary instruments, section-level instrument evolution, groove, bass, percussion, textures, and spatial effects. This representation allows the model to follow not only a global style, but also the musical development of the song over time. ## Hybrid-LM MiniMax Music 3 uses a hierarchical autoregressive architecture that separates global musical modeling from local acoustic modeling. - The **Global LLM (8B)** predicts the first RVQ codebook frame by frame and models the song's long-range semantic and structural progression. - The **Local LLM (0.6B)** predicts the remaining acoustic codebooks within each frame and restores fine-grained acoustic information. The Global LLM is initialized from Qwen3-8B. During training, its embedding and output layers are first adapted to semantic music tokens. The Global and Local LLMs are then jointly trained to model all RVQ codebooks. ## Continuous Hidden-State Synthesis Instead of decoding only from discrete RVQ tokens, the synthesis module fuses the final hidden states of the Global and Local LLMs. These continuous representations preserve richer acoustic information for vocal articulation, instrumental texture, and temporal continuity. The synthesis path is: ```text Global and Local LLM hidden states ↓ Hidden-state fusion ↓ Flow Matching (2.4B) ↓ Flow-VAE latent ↓ Flow-VAE Decoder (123M) ↓ 32 kHz stereo audio ``` The Flow-VAE architecture is adapted from MiniMax Speech and retrained for the dynamic range and spectral characteristics of music. ## Music Tokenizer The training tokenizer uses eight layers of Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ): - The first semantic codebook contains **16,384** entries and captures the core musical semantics and structure. - The remaining seven acoustic codebooks contain **1,024** entries each and represent residual acoustic details. Training first optimizes the semantic codebook, then jointly trains all eight codebooks. At inference time, waveform synthesis uses the fused LLM hidden states and does not require the discrete tokenizer decoder. ## How to Use MiniMax Music 3 is supported by [SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni). Follow the official [installation guide](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/get_started/installation.html) to prepare the runtime environment. ### Download the Model ```bash hf download MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3 --local-dir /path/to/minimax_ttm ``` We recommend the following inference frameworks to serve the model: - [SGLang](https://docs.sglang.io/) \- see [cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/minimax_music3.html) - [diffusers](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers) \- see [diffusers docs](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/minimax-music3-integration/docs/source/en/api/pipelines/minimax_music3.md) - [ComfyUI](https://github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI) see [comfyUI tutorials](https://docs.comfy.org/tutorials/audio/minimax/minimax-music-3) ### Serve with SGLang-Omni ```bash sgl-omni serve --model-path MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3 --port 8000 ``` ### Generate Music The service uses the shared speech API. Put the lyrics in `input` and the music description in `instructions`. Put lyric structure tags such as `[Verse]` and `[Chorus]` on their own lines. ```bash curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/audio/speech \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3", "input": "[Verse]\nMorning light filtering through the pine\n[Chorus]\nSoftly the world begins to breathe", "instructions": "A warm acoustic pop song with intimate female vocals, fingerpicked guitar, soft piano, and a gradual emotional build into a wide final chorus.", "response_format": "wav", "seed": 7, "max_new_tokens": 750, "stream": false }' \ --output minimax_music3.wav ``` `max_new_tokens` sets the maximum number of audio frames at 25 frames per second. Generation may finish before this limit when the model emits an end-of-audio token. The response is a 32 kHz, 16-bit stereo WAV file. ### Reproducible Example The following end-to-end example contains the complete lyrics, music description, and generation parameters used to produce the reference audio. | Use case | Request | Result | |---|---|---| | Text-to-music | [View script](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3/blob/main/scripts/end_to_end/minimax_ttm_test.py) | [minimax_ttm.wav](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3/blob/main/assets/minimax_ttm.wav) | ## 🧨 Diffusers MiniMax Music 3 is available as a [diffusers](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers) modular pipeline. Until [huggingface/diffusers#14456](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/pull/14456) is merged, install diffusers from the PR commit: The snippet below fits 24GB+ VRAM GPUs ```bash pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers@dafe3733fcfdbf3c48915fe77be3aef65b5d6a2d transformers accelerate soundfile ``` ```python import soundfile as sf import torch from diffusers import ModularPipeline pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3") pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16) pipe.to("cuda") lyrics = """[verse] Morning light filtering through the pine Every quiet street is yours and mine [chorus] Softly the world begins to breathe""" prompt = ( "Genre: acoustic pop. BPM: 96. Key: C major. Warm and intimate, building gently into the chorus. " "Vocals: soft female lead, close and breathy, light stacked harmonies in the chorus. " "Arrangement: fingerpicked guitar and soft piano; brushed drums and upright bass enter in the chorus." ) audio = pipe( prompt=prompt, lyrics=lyrics, audio_duration=60.0, generator=torch.Generator("cuda").manual_seed(7), output="audios", )[0] sf.write("song.wav", audio.T.float().cpu().numpy(), pipe.sampling_rate) ``` ### Low VRAM The full precision fits under 24GB of VRAM. With automatic CPU offloading, generation takes in ~22 GB; additionally streaming the language model layer by layer makes it fit even 8 GB video cards: ```python import torch from diffusers import ComponentsManager, ModularPipeline from diffusers.hooks import apply_group_offloading manager = ComponentsManager() manager.enable_auto_cpu_offload(device="cuda") pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3", components_manager=manager) pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16) # Only needed below ~22 GB of VRAM — slower, but fits in 8 GB. apply_group_offloading( pipe.language_model, onload_device=torch.device("cuda"), offload_type="leaf_level", use_stream=True ) ``` ## Prompt Enhancement A concise natural-language description can be used directly. For richer prompts and more precise control, use the provided [`music-caption-rewriter`](https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-Music3/tree/main/skills/music-caption-rewriter) skill to expand it into a Structured Caption containing `Global Metadata`, `Vocal Details`, and `Arrangement`. The skill preserves musical instructions attached to lyric section tags in the arrangement description while keeping the lyric text in the lyrics input. ```bash npx skills add MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-Music3 --skill music-caption-rewriter ``` ## Limitations - Inference requires CUDA. - Only non-streaming generation is currently supported. - The tokenized text prompt is limited to 5,000 tokens. - Audio generation is limited to 9,000 acoustic frames. - Section tags and music descriptions provide generative control rather than strict symbolic guarantees. The generated tempo, key, instrumentation, lyrics, and song structure may not always match every requested detail exactly. ## Contact Us Contact us at [model@minimax.io](mailto:model@minimax.io).

Ming-3.0-audio-tiny

Hear clearly. Understand deeply. Act intelligently.

Ming-3.0-audio-tiny is a compact native audio-language model from inclusionAI. It accepts audio together with text instructions and supports speech recognition, spoken question answering, audio understanding, audio reasoning, and optional synthesized-speech responses.
GitHub · 🤖 ModelScope · 🤗 Flash · 🤗 Tiny · 💻 Examples
## Model Summary | Property | Description | | --- | --- | | Developer | inclusionAI | | Model type | Compact native audio-language Mixture-of-Experts model | | Parameters | 9.3B total parameters, 2.7B activated per inference step | | Inputs | Audio and text instructions | | Outputs | Text, or text with optional synthesized speech | | Primary languages | Chinese and English, including varied accents and dialects | | License | MIT | ## Highlights - **Efficient audio intelligence:** Provides speech and audio understanding in a compact Mixture-of-Experts model. - **Complex speech recognition:** Handles Chinese and English speech, dialects, accents, noisy environments, and multi-speaker recordings. - **Long-audio understanding:** Comprehends and analyzes long-form recordings. - **Multidimensional perception:** Understands speech, non-speech sounds, acoustic scenes, and music. - **Audio reasoning:** Answers questions and performs reasoning over audio content. - **Audio interaction:** Produces text responses and can optionally synthesize speech with built-in voices or a reference voice. ## Architecture Ming-3.0-audio-tiny combines an audio encoder and projector with a compact Mixture-of-Experts language backbone. An optional Talker generates speech responses from the model's output. ## Quick Start with Transformers The model uses custom Transformers code. Review the repository code before enabling `trust_remote_code=True`. ```bash git clone https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash.git cd Ming-3.0-audio-flash python -m venv .venv-transformers source .venv-transformers/bin/activate pip install -r requirements-transformers.txt ``` ### Audio Understanding ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny \ --prompt "Please answer the question in the audio." ``` ### Speech Recognition ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny \ --task asr \ --max-new-tokens 256 \ --no-repeat-ngram-size 10 ``` The validated ASR prompt asks the model to identify the spoken language and place a tab between the language label and transcription. ### Direct Python Usage ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny" audio_path = "examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained( model_id, trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=False, ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", trust_remote_code=True, ).eval() messages = [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "audio", "audio": audio_path}, {"type": "text", "text": "Please answer the question in the audio."}, ], } ] inputs = processor(messages).to(model.device) inputs["audio_feats"] = inputs["audio_feats"].to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=512, do_sample=False, ) generated_ids = output_ids[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :] response = processor.decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True).strip() print(response) ``` ## Speech Output The Talker example supports built-in voices and reference-audio voice prompting: ```bash python examples/transformers_thinker_talker.py \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny \ --audio examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --voice US_Stella \ --output output.wav ``` See the [voice guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/docs/voices.md) for available voice names, invocation rules, and reference-audio usage. ## Serving ### vLLM-Omni Text output or ASR uses the Tiny Thinker on one GPU: ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny MING_MODEL_VARIANT=tiny MING_OUTPUT_MODE=text \ ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` For synthesized-speech output, select the full-audio profile: ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny MING_MODEL_VARIANT=tiny MING_OUTPUT_MODE=audio \ ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The reference full-audio profile places the Thinker on GPU 0 and the Talker on GPU 1. Select the deployment YAML that matches text-only, ASR, or Talker output. See the [deployment guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/README.md#vllm-omni) for details. Select an IP or registered voice with the vLLM-Omni client's `--voice` option: ```bash python examples/vllm_omni_audio_chat.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --audio-response \ --voice US_Stella \ --output-audio outputs/answer.wav ``` The client sends this selection as Chat Completions `audio.voice: {"id": "..."}`. vLLM-Omni uses the built-in IP voice `灵小柔` when no voice is specified. The model directory also provides `灵楷` and `US_James` as preset reference voices under `voice_presets/voice_audio/`, with their matching transcripts in `voice_presets/voice_prompts.json`. Both names are also available as built-in IP voices. ### SGLang ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny MING_MODEL_VARIANT=tiny CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \ ./scripts/serve_sglang.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The validated Tiny SGLang profile uses one GPU and provides text output. See the [SGLang example](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/examples/sglang_audio_chat.py) for client usage. ### SGLang-Omni [SGLang-Omni](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/) serves transcription, audio chat, and speech synthesis from one server. The Tiny checkpoint fits on a single GPU; `--talker.gpu 0` colocates speech synthesis with the other stages: ```bash sgl-omni serve --model-path inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny --talker.gpu 0 ``` The server exposes OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/transcriptions`, `/v1/audio/speech`, and `/v1/chat/completions` endpoints. The [SGLang-Omni cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/ming3_audio.html) shows client examples; the same requests work with the Tiny model name. ## Evaluation The shared benchmark figures below include results for both Ming-3.0-audio-tiny and Ming-3.0-audio-flash. ### Speech Recognition

# YuE2-3B · MLX 4-bit

[YuE2-3B](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B) quantized to 4-bit for
[MLX](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx). It turns lyrics and a style prompt
into a full song, vocals and accompaniment, on Apple silicon, including iPhone.

All the weights together take **2.15 GB**. The two transformer models shrink from 7.2 GB in bf16 to 2.0 GB. A 30-second song
generates in **82 seconds on an iPhone 17 Pro Max** running iOS 26.6.

Published by [Milliwatt Labs](https://milliwattlabs.com). This is an unofficial
conversion. For the model itself, its training and its benchmarks, see the
[original model card](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B).

## Samples

Generated on a Mac mini (M4) with this 4-bit model. More on [EM Radio](https://radio.transistorkit.com/), streaming 24/7.

| Song | Artist | Genre | Listen |
|---|---|---|---|
| Better Off | Kira Nova | Pop | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/milliwattlabs/YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit/resolve/main/samples/better-off.m4a"></audio> |
| Signal | Ada Ray | Top 40 | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/milliwattlabs/YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit/resolve/main/samples/signal.m4a"></audio> |
| Coal Miner's Blood | Boone Harlan | Country | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/milliwattlabs/YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit/resolve/main/samples/coal-miners-blood.m4a"></audio> |

| Pressure | Blaze Meridian | Hip-hop | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/milliwattlabs/YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit/resolve/main/samples/pressure.m4a"></audio> |

## Apps

Free apps built on this model. [ChorusPop](https://choruspop.com) adds stems, MIDI import and export, and an instrumental mode.

| Platform | App |
|---|---|
| iPhone and iPad | [ChorusPop (TestFlight beta)](https://testflight.apple.com/join/b7j7z3CT) |
| Mac | [ChorusPop for Mac (zip)](https://choruspop.com/download/ChorusPop-1.0.zip) |
| Android | [ChorusPop for Android (APK beta)](https://choruspop.com/beta/ChorusPop-android.apk). Uses YuE2 weights converted for Android, not these MLX files. |

## Files

| Directory | What | Precision | Size |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `weights/ar-4bit/` | Autoregressive LM (Qwen3 architecture, 28 layers). Writes the ABC score, then the audio codec tokens. | 4-bit, group size 64 | 1.22 GB |
| `weights/nar-4bit/` | Non-autoregressive velocity model. Turns codec tokens into audio latents. | 4-bit, group size 64; latent interface (`llm2vae`, `vae2llm`, `time_embedder`) kept in bf16 | 0.80 GB |
| `weights/vae-decoder/` | Oobleck decoder from [YuE2-Vae](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-Vae). Turns 25 Hz latents into 48 kHz stereo audio. | fp16 | 0.13 GB |

Also in `weights/`: the tokenizer (`qwen.tiktoken`) and the sampling settings
(`yue2_generation_config.json`). At the repo root: the MLX runner (`yue2_mlx.py`,
`run_song.py`), `requirements.txt`, and the license files.

Quantization is MLX's affine `mx.quantize` (4 bits, group size 64). The AR
directory is a standard `qwen3` MLX checkpoint with a `quantization` block in
`config.json`.

## Changes from the original

As the CC BY-NC 4.0 license requires, here is what was changed:

- The AR and NAR linear weights are quantized to 4-bit (affine, group size 64).
  Norms and the NAR latent interface stay in bf16.
- In the VAE decoder, weight normalization is folded into plain weights
  (`g · v / ‖v‖`), stored in fp16. Only the decoder is included.
- The tensors were rearranged into three MLX checkpoints. No weights were
  retrained or fine-tuned.

## Quality compared with bf16

Each number compares this conversion with the original bf16 weights on the
same prompt and seed. That's one song, so treat it as a fidelity check, not a
benchmark.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| AR codec tokens: top-1 agreement with bf16 (teacher-forced) | 82.9% |
| AR codec KL divergence from bf16 | 0.023 |
| AR codec perplexity, 4-bit / bf16 | 39.3 / 40.0 |
| AR score (ABC) tokens: top-1 agreement | 98.8% |
| NAR velocity cosine vs bf16 | 0.9965 |
| Rendered latents, cosine vs bf16 (same codec tokens and noise) | 0.985 |
| VAE decoder fp16 vs fp32 | 60.8 dB SNR |
| Free-running song from lyrics | Finishes normally (emits the end-of-music token), 560 score + 1,056 codec tokens |

For the same seed, the 4-bit model doesn't reproduce the bf16 song note for
note. Its songs drift into a different, equally valid performance.

## On a Mac

One full song, measured on a Mac mini (M4, 16 GB) running macOS 26.5 with
MLX 0.32.2. The model ended the song on its own after 61.9 seconds of audio.

| Stage | Seconds |
|---|---:|
| Load (tokenizer, AR, NAR) | 1.7 |
| Score (ABC), 691 tokens at 80 tokens/s | 9.6 |
| Codec tokens, 1,548 at 85 tokens/s | 19.0 |
| NAR (codec → latents), 32 steps | 116.1 |
| VAE decode | 5.2 |
| **Total** | **152** |

Peak MLX memory was 3.5 GB, during VAE decode.

## On iPhone

A 30-second clip, measured on an iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 26.6:

| Stage | Seconds |
|---|---:|
| Load (tokenizer, AR) | 0.6 |
| Score (ABC), 26 tokens/s | 23.2 |
| Codec tokens (750), 41 tokens/s | 18.8 |
| NAR (codec → latents) | 34.3 |
| VAE decode | 4.3 |
| **Total** | **81.6** |

- **Memory:** peak footprint 1.9 GB during generation and 3.6 GB during VAE decode.
- **Thermal state:** nominal the whole run.
- **Latents** match the reference implementation's latents at cosine 0.9995 for
  the same tokens.

## Usage

**Requirements**

- An Apple silicon Mac (M1 or later). Intel Macs are not supported.
- 8 GB of memory minimum; 16 GB recommended. A 3½-minute song peaks at 3.5 GB.
- macOS 14 or later.
- Python 3.10 or later.

Tested on a Mac mini (M4, 16 GB) with macOS 26, Python 3.12, `mlx` 0.32.2
and `mlx-lm` 0.29.1.

Got it running on another Mac? Let us know in the
[Community](https://huggingface.co/milliwattlabs/YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit/discussions)
tab which Mac it was and how long a song took.

```bash
pip install mlx mlx-lm numpy tiktoken huggingface_hub
hf download milliwattlabs/YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit --local-dir YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit
cd YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit

python run_song.py --weights weights --out out \
  --style "upbeat indie pop, warm female lead vocal, acoustic guitar, light drums" \
  --lyrics "$(cat lyrics.txt)" --seed 11
```

The song is written to `out/song.wav` (48 kHz stereo), and the score to
`out/abc.txt`. Lyrics use `[verse]` and `[chorus]` section tags. The same seed
gives a different song than the original PyTorch release, because MLX uses a
different random number generator.

`--cot` picks how much of the score the model writes before the audio:
`full` (melody and chords, the default), `melody`, or `off`.

## Limitations

- **Non-commercial only.** The license comes from the original weights (see below).
- Everything in the original card's limitations applies here too.
- The runner generates a song in a single context window. Songs longer than
  one window, which the original splits into chunks, aren't supported yet.
- The quality figures above cover one prompt and one seed. Listen before relying on it.
- Only the decoder half of the VAE is included, so this conversion can't
  encode reference audio. Cover mode, which needs the encoder, isn't supported.
  <!-- TODO: confirm cover mode is out of scope -->
