# TTM-HumanPref: G-Clef FluxAudio-S checkpoint (ICME 2026 ATTM Grand Challenge)

Final submitted checkpoint of **Team G-Clef** for the Efficiency track of the [ICME 2026 Academic Text-to-Music Grand Challenge](https://ntu-musicailab.github.io/ICME26-ATTM-Grand-Challenge/).

A ~120M-parameter FluxAudio-S rectified-flow model, trained from scratch on the challenge's CC-licensed instrumental MTG-Jamendo subset, then refined with human-preference reward conditioning, expert iteration, and a short CRPO preference fine-tune.

- **Paper:** [Improving Text-to-Music Generation with Human Preference Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21670)
- **Code:** [github.com/yonghyunk1m/TTM-HumanPref](https://github.com/yonghyunk1m/TTM-HumanPref)
- **Demo:** [TTM-HumanPref Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/yonghyunk1m/TTM-HumanPref)

## Files

| File | Size | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `gclef_crpoA_fluxaudio_s.pt` | 483 MB | Final CRPO-A checkpoint, used for both submissions |

SHA-256: `0cfb8295fbd695a99c7a2599363a465fdc28a94f39c8d43faf7487461e5e15f2`

This file is identical to the asset of the GitHub release [`v1.0-icme2026`](https://github.com/yonghyunk1m/TTM-HumanPref/releases/tag/v1.0-icme2026).

## Usage

Inference runs through the code repository, on top of the official challenge baseline. See the [GitHub README](https://github.com/yonghyunk1m/TTM-HumanPref) for setup.

```bash
python run.py download-weights          # fetches this checkpoint and verifies its SHA-256
python run.py reproduce --seed 42       # Submission 1
python run.py reproduce --seed 55       # Submission 2
```

Both submissions come from this single checkpoint and differ only in the generation seed. Inference uses joint classifier-free guidance on text and reward, 25 Euler steps, and the prompt prefix `"high quality instrumental music, "`.

## Intended use and limitations

Research and non-commercial use. The model generates instrumental music only (~10 s, 44.1 kHz) and was trained on a limited instrumental subset of MTG-Jamendo, so its stylistic coverage reflects that data.

# 👑 JJ coders Suna AI v1.0 — Official Halloween 2026 Flagship Foundation Model

**JJ coders Suna AI v1.0** is an open-source **48 kHz stereo vocal and instrumental music generation system** engineered by **JJ Coders Group (Johan Jomet)**. It combines a **5-Billion Parameter Continuous Flow-Matching Diffusion Transformer (`ACE-Step 1.5 XL SFT`)**, **`Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B`** lyric/phonetic conditioning, **14 Per-Genre Rank-64 DiT LoRA Experts**, a **15.8M-Parameter 12-Block Dilated ResNet-SE Masterpiece Critic (`SunaV1TitanMasterpieceNet`)**, and **48 kHz Stereo Melodic Soul Guides**.

* 🌐 **Official Website:** [suna.jjcoders.com](https://suna.jjcoders.com)
* 🎛️ **Live A100 Gradio Studio:** [huggingface.co/spaces/johanjomet/suna-ai-studio](https://huggingface.co/spaces/johanjomet/suna-ai-studio)
* 📦 **Model Hub Repository:** [huggingface.co/jjcoders/suna-v1](https://huggingface.co/jjcoders/suna-v1)

---

## 🚀 Key Architectural Breakthroughs in `Suna AI v1.0`

| Architectural Layer | Legacy Raw Open-Source Diffusion | JJ coders Suna AI v1.0 Flagship |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Vocal Pitch & Melody (`210–4,200 Hz`)** | Flat 1-note monotone "reading text aloud" | **Legato Melodic Soul Guide + `+12st` Octave Chorus Belt (`1.8 Oct` F0 range)** |
| **Intro Rhythm Lock (`0:00–0:15`)** | 20–35s of beatless silence or random noise | **Locked-in `0:00` Sub-Bass & Drum Pocket (`99.4%` groove lock)** |
| **Lyric & Phonetic Articulation** | 20s `"Oh-woah"` scream loops & shouted `[Drop]!` tags | **Syllable-Paced Phonetic Aligner + Multilingual G2P (`en`, `ml`, `fr`, `es`)** |
| **Candidate Selection** | Single blind random seed | **15.8M-Param `SunaV1TitanMasterpieceNet` (12 Dilated ResBlocks + SE)** |
| **Audio Fidelity & Mastering** | 16–32 kHz mono/muddy output | **True 48 kHz Stereo Oobleck VAE + `-14 LUFS` Mid-Side Mastering** |

---

* `model.safetensors` & `suna_v1_lora_experts.safetensors` — Official SafeTensors weights containing all 14 Rank-64 DiT LoRA Experts and the 15.8M-parameter `SunaV1TitanMasterpieceNet` Critic.
* `JJ_coders_Suna_AI_v1_Q4_K_M.gguf` & `JJ_coders_Suna_AI_v1_3_Q4_K_M.gguf` — Official binary GGUF v3 packages for local/edge runtimes.

--- license: apache-2.0 language: - en - zh library_name: transformers pipeline_tag: audio-text-to-text tags: - music - music-understanding - audio - audio-language-model - moss - moss-music - lyrics-asr - music-captioning - chord-recognition --- # MOSS-Music

English | 简体中文

**MOSS-Music** is an open-source **music understanding model** from [MOSI.AI](https://mosi.cn/#hero), the [OpenMOSS team](https://www.open-moss.com/), and [Shanghai Innovation Institute](https://www.sii.edu.cn/). Built on the same audio backbone as [MOSS-Audio](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Audio), MOSS-Music is further specialised on music via dedicated continual pre-training and supervised fine-tuning — targeting **musical captioning, lyrics ASR, structural analysis, chord / key / tempo reasoning, and long-form musical question answering**. In this release, we provide **two 8B models**: **MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct** and **MOSS-Music-8B-Thinking**. The Instruct variant is optimised for direct instruction following on musical prompts, while the Thinking variant provides stronger chain-of-thought reasoning for musical analysis. ## News * 2026.05.01: 🎉🎉🎉 We have released [MOSS-Music](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Music). * 2026.05.01: 🎉🎉🎉 We have released [MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline](https://github.com/wx9songs/MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline) for large-scale music data annotation and processing. ## Contents - [Introduction](#introduction) - [Model Architecture](#model-architecture) - [DeepStack Cross-Layer Feature Injection](#deepstack-cross-layer-feature-injection) - [Time-Aware Representation](#time-aware-representation) - [Released Models](#released-models) - [Music Data Pipeline](#music-data-pipeline) - [Evaluation](#evaluation) - [Quickstart](#quickstart) - [Environment Setup](#environment-setup) - [SGLang Serving](#sglang-serving) - [Gradio App](#gradio-app) - [More Information](#more-information) - [LICENSE](#license) - [Citation](#citation) ## Introduction Music is not just audio plus lyrics — understanding it requires perceiving harmonic structure, rhythm, timbre, instrumentation, performance nuance, and the textual content of the lyrics, and reasoning about them jointly across time. **MOSS-Music** is built to unify these capabilities within a single model. - **Lyrics ASR & time-aligned transcription**: Accurate singing ASR with sentence- and word-level timestamps, robust to backing tracks. - **Musical captioning & tagging**: Natural-language descriptions of mood, genre, instrumentation, production style, and emotional trajectory. - **Key / tempo / chord reasoning**: Identifies musical key, beats, downbeats, and chord progressions, including timestamped chord transcription. - **Structural analysis**: Segments a song into intro / verse / chorus / bridge / outro and reasons about repetition and contrast. - **Instrument & voice recognition**: Identifies prominent instruments and singing voices (solo / chorus, gender, register). - **Musical QA and long-form analysis**: Open-ended question answering grounded in a full track, including chain-of-thought reasoning in the *Thinking* variant.

## Model Architecture MOSS-Music inherits the MOSS-Audio modular design, comprising three components: an audio encoder, a modality adapter, and a large language model. Raw audio is first encoded by **MOSS-Audio-Encoder** into continuous temporal representations at **12.5 Hz**, which are then projected into the language model's embedding space through the adapter and finally consumed by the LLM for auto-regressive text generation. Rather than relying on off-the-shelf audio frontends, we train a dedicated encoder from scratch to obtain more robust acoustic representations, tighter temporal alignment, and better extensibility across musical styles, singing, and non-speech acoustic content. ### DeepStack Cross-Layer Feature Injection Using only the encoder's top-layer features tends to lose low-level prosody, transient events, and local time-frequency structure. To address this, we adopt a **DeepStack**-inspired cross-layer injection module between the encoder and the language model: in addition to the encoder's final-layer output, features from earlier and intermediate layers are selected, independently projected, and injected into the language model's early layers, preserving multi-granularity information from low-level acoustic details to high-level semantic abstractions. This design is especially well-suited for music understanding, as it helps retain rhythm, timbre, transients, and instrumental texture — information that a single high-level representation cannot fully capture, yet is critical for chord recognition, structural analysis, and nuanced musical description. ### Time-Aware Representation Time is a critical dimension in music understanding. To enhance explicit temporal awareness, we adopt a **time-marker insertion** strategy during pre-training: explicit time tokens are inserted between audio frame representations at fixed time intervals to indicate temporal positions. This design enables the model to learn "what happened when" within a unified text generation framework, naturally supporting timestamped lyrics ASR, beat / downbeat localisation, section boundary detection, and long-song retrospective QA. Building on the MOSS-Audio backbone, MOSS-Music is further enhanced through: - **continual pre-training** on a large, diverse music corpus produced by the data annotation and processing pipeline [`MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline`](https://github.com/wx9songs/MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline), with an emphasis on singing, lyrics, and full-song coverage; - **supervised fine-tuning (SFT)** on music-centric instruction data covering captioning, lyrics ASR, chord / key / structural analysis, and long-form musical QA; - additional **reasoning tuning** for the *Thinking* variant. ## Released Models | Model | Audio Encoder | LLM Backbone | Total Size | Hugging Face | ModelScope | |---|---|---|---:|---|---| | **MOSS‑Music‑8B‑Instruct** | MOSS-Audio-Encoder | Qwen3-8B | ~9.1B | [![Hugging Face](https://img.shields.io/badge/Huggingface-Model-orange?logo=huggingface)](https://huggingface.co/OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct) | [![ModelScope](https://img.shields.io/badge/ModelScope-Model-624AFF)](https://modelscope.cn/models/openmoss/MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct) | | **MOSS‑Music‑8B‑Thinking** | MOSS-Audio-Encoder | Qwen3-8B | ~9.1B | [![Hugging Face](https://img.shields.io/badge/Huggingface-Model-orange?logo=huggingface)](https://huggingface.co/OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Music-8B-Thinking) | [![ModelScope](https://img.shields.io/badge/ModelScope-Model-624AFF)](https://modelscope.cn/models/openmoss/MOSS-Music-8B-Thinking) | > Smaller (4B) variants and additional sizes may follow. Stay tuned! ## Music Data Pipeline The training data used by MOSS-Music is produced by an end-to-end pipeline that goes from raw audio to chat-formatted training samples. That pipeline is available at [`MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline`](https://github.com/wx9songs/MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline), which hosts duration detection, MIR feature extraction, song-structure segmentation, lyrics ASR, metadata cleanup, and ALM-driven caption / query generation with models such as Qwen3-Omni, MusicFlamingo, and other audio-language models.

## Evaluation We evaluate MOSS-Music on a diverse suite of public music understanding benchmarks. Key results: - **Music QA and understanding**: **MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct** achieves **80.38** average accuracy across **8 public music QA benchmarks** (excluding the three NSynth note-recognition tracks), ranking first among all compared models in our current evaluation set. - **Music captioning**: In our preliminary **GPT-5.4-as-a-Judge** evaluation, the MOSS-Music series leads both caption benchmarks, with `MOSS-Music-8B-Thinking` reaching **4.53** on `MusicCaps` and `MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct` reaching **4.58** on `SDD`. - **Lyrics ASR for singing voice**: **MOSS-Music-8B-Thinking** achieves the best average lyrics recognition error across `MUSDB18`, `MIR-1K` and `Opencpop` (**15.88%** avg WER/CER), clearly ahead of all compared audio-language baselines including `Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview`, `MusicFlamingo` and `Qwen3-Omni`. Detailed timestamped-ASR results will be released in a later update. - **Chord transcription**: MOSS-Music supports chord transcription, including timestamped chord transcription for harmonic analysis, accompaniment reference, and related downstream use cases. English | 简体中文

**MOSS-Music** is an open-source **music understanding model** from [MOSI.AI](https://mosi.cn/#hero), the [OpenMOSS team](https://www.open-moss.com/), and [Shanghai Innovation Institute](https://www.sii.edu.cn/). Built on the same audio backbone as [MOSS-Audio](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Audio), MOSS-Music is further specialised on music via dedicated continual pre-training and supervised fine-tuning — targeting **musical captioning, lyrics ASR, structural analysis, chord / key / tempo reasoning, and long-form musical question answering**. In this release, we provide **two 8B models**: **MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct** and **MOSS-Music-8B-Thinking**. The Instruct variant is optimised for direct instruction following on musical prompts, while the Thinking variant provides stronger chain-of-thought reasoning for musical analysis. ## News * 2026.05.01: 🎉🎉🎉 We have released [MOSS-Music](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Music). * 2026.05.01: 🎉🎉🎉 We have released [MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline](https://github.com/wx9songs/MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline) for large-scale music data annotation and processing. ## Contents - [Released Models](#released-models) - [Music Data Pipeline](#music-data-pipeline) - [Evaluation](#evaluation) - [Quickstart](#quickstart) - [Environment Setup](#environment-setup) - [SGLang Serving](#sglang-serving) - [Gradio App](#gradio-app) - [More Information](#more-information) - [LICENSE](#license) - [Citation](#citation) ## Introduction Music is not just audio plus lyrics — understanding it requires perceiving harmonic structure, rhythm, timbre, instrumentation, performance nuance, and the textual content of the lyrics, and reasoning about them jointly across time. **MOSS-Music** is built to unify these capabilities within a single model. - **Lyrics ASR & time-aligned transcription**: Accurate singing ASR with sentence- and word-level timestamps, robust to backing tracks. - **Musical captioning & tagging**: Natural-language descriptions of mood, genre, instrumentation, production style, and emotional trajectory. - **Key / tempo / chord reasoning**: Identifies musical key, beats, downbeats, and chord progressions, including timestamped chord transcription. - **Structural analysis**: Segments a song into intro / verse / chorus / bridge / outro and reasons about repetition and contrast. - **Instrument & voice recognition**: Identifies prominent instruments and singing voices (solo / chorus, gender, register). - **Musical QA and long-form analysis**: Open-ended question answering grounded in a full track, including chain-of-thought reasoning in the *Thinking* variant.

## Model Architecture MOSS-Music inherits the MOSS-Audio modular design, comprising three components: an audio encoder, a modality adapter, and a large language model. Raw audio is first encoded by **MOSS-Audio-Encoder** into continuous temporal representations at **12.5 Hz**, which are then projected into the language model's embedding space through the adapter and finally consumed by the LLM for auto-regressive text generation. Rather than relying on off-the-shelf audio frontends, we train a dedicated encoder from scratch to obtain more robust acoustic representations, tighter temporal alignment, and better extensibility across musical styles, singing, and non-speech acoustic content. ### DeepStack Cross-Layer Feature Injection Using only the encoder's top-layer features tends to lose low-level prosody, transient events, and local time-frequency structure. To address this, we adopt a **DeepStack**-inspired cross-layer injection module between the encoder and the language model: in addition to the encoder's final-layer output, features from earlier and intermediate layers are selected, independently projected, and injected into the language model's early layers, preserving multi-granularity information from low-level acoustic details to high-level semantic abstractions. This design is especially well-suited for music understanding, as it helps retain rhythm, timbre, transients, and instrumental texture — information that a single high-level representation cannot fully capture, yet is critical for chord recognition, structural analysis, and nuanced musical description. ### Time-Aware Representation Time is a critical dimension in music understanding. To enhance explicit temporal awareness, we adopt a **time-marker insertion** strategy during pre-training: explicit time tokens are inserted between audio frame representations at fixed time intervals to indicate temporal positions. This design enables the model to learn "what happened when" within a unified text generation framework, naturally supporting timestamped lyrics ASR, beat / downbeat localisation, section boundary detection, and long-song retrospective QA. Building on the MOSS-Audio backbone, MOSS-Music is further enhanced through: - **continual pre-training** on a large, diverse music corpus produced by the data annotation and processing pipeline [`MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline`](https://github.com/wx9songs/MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline), with an emphasis on singing, lyrics, and full-song coverage; - **supervised fine-tuning (SFT)** on music-centric instruction data covering captioning, lyrics ASR, chord / key / structural analysis, and long-form musical QA; - additional **reasoning tuning** for the *Thinking* variant. ## Released Models | Model | Audio Encoder | LLM Backbone | Total Size | Hugging Face | ModelScope | |---|---|---|---:|---|---| | **MOSS‑Music‑8B‑Instruct** | MOSS-Audio-Encoder | Qwen3-8B | ~9.1B | [![Hugging Face](https://img.shields.io/badge/Huggingface-Model-orange?logo=huggingface)](https://huggingface.co/OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct) | [![ModelScope](https://img.shields.io/badge/ModelScope-Model-624AFF)](https://modelscope.cn/models/openmoss/MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct) | | **MOSS‑Music‑8B‑Thinking** | MOSS-Audio-Encoder | Qwen3-8B | ~9.1B | [![Hugging Face](https://img.shields.io/badge/Huggingface-Model-orange?logo=huggingface)](https://huggingface.co/OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Music-8B-Thinking) | [![ModelScope](https://img.shields.io/badge/ModelScope-Model-624AFF)](https://modelscope.cn/models/openmoss/MOSS-Music-8B-Thinking) | > Smaller (4B) variants and additional sizes may follow. That pipeline is available at [`MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline`](https://github.com/wx9songs/MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline), which hosts duration detection, MIR feature extraction, song-structure segmentation, lyrics ASR, metadata cleanup, and ALM-driven caption / query generation with models such as Qwen3-Omni, MusicFlamingo, and other audio-language models.

Detailed timestamped-ASR results will be released in a later update. - **Chord transcription**: MOSS-Music supports chord transcription, including timestamped chord transcription for harmonic analysis, accompaniment reference, and related downstream use cases. Detailed benchmark results will be released in a later update.

# Ultravox-Qwen3.6-27B (Base)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **This is an early research base checkpoint** — English-only, trained on clean studio audio with **no telephony data**. If you want the model for actual voice-agent or phone-call use, get **[ultravox-qwen3.6-27b-v2](https://huggingface.co/QuantumDesk-AI/ultravox-qwen3.6-27b-v2)** — the production successor trained through Phase 1B (telephony augmentation) + Phase 2 (entity-dense + dialogue data), with published benchmarks. This checkpoint is published for reproducibility and research on the adapter-training recipe.

A speech-language model built on the Ultravox architecture, using **Qwen 3.6-27B** as the language backbone and **Whisper-large-v3-turbo** as the audio encoder. Pretrained by [Quantum Desk LTD](https://generalconcepts.ai) for real-time voice agent applications.

Unlike a cascaded ASR → LLM pipeline, this model consumes raw audio embeddings directly into the LLM's token stream — eliminating the transcription hop and cutting **200-400 ms** of latency per turn.

## Model Details

| | |
|---|---|
| Base LLM | [`Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B`](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B) (27B params, hybrid GDN/DeltaNet attention) |
| Audio encoder | [`openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo`](https://huggingface.co/openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo) |
| Projection adapter | Swiglu MLP, `stack_factor=8`, `hidden_size=5120` |
| Trainable params | ~100 M (projector + Whisper LoRA `r=8`) |
| Frozen params | 27 B (LLM never gradient-updated) |
| Training precision | bfloat16 |
| Recommended serve precision | Base LLM in **FP8**, projector + LoRA in bf16 |
| Language | English (base checkpoint) |
| Context length | 131 072 tokens |

## Training

- **Loss**: KL divergence to teacher (temperature 2.0)
- **Steps**: 10 000 (loss converged near step ~500, remaining steps refined the projection)
- **Effective batch**: 16 (8 × 2 gradient accumulation)
- **LR**: 5e-4 cosine → 5e-5, 500-step warmup
- **Optimizer**: AdamW
- **Hardware**: 1 × NVIDIA B200 (180 GB HBM3e), single-GPU, no FSDP
- **Wall-clock**: ~6 h 30 min
- **Whisper adaptation**: LoRA rank 8 on Whisper `k_proj`, `q_proj`, `linear_k`, `linear_q`

### Training data

English audio-transcription and audio-continuation mix (~10 datasets):

- `fixie-ai/librispeech_asr` (clean + other, continuation + transcription)
- `fixie-ai/peoplespeech-clean`
- `fixie-ai/gigaspeech-xl`
- `fixie-ai/commonvoice-en`

**This is an English-only base checkpoint.** Multilingual and phone-quality audio training were deliberately excluded to accelerate iteration and reduce cost. That broader training (Phase 1B telephony mix + Phase 2 domain data) has since shipped as **[ultravox-qwen3.6-27b-v2](https://huggingface.co/QuantumDesk-AI/ultravox-qwen3.6-27b-v2)**.

## Evaluation

Training-time metrics on `fixie-ai/librispeech-clean-transcription` (validation, 256 samples):

| Step | Eval loss |
|---|---|
| 500 | 0.442 |
| 5 000 | 0.383 |
| 9 000 | 0.381 |
| 10 000 (final) | **0.372** |

For reference, Fixie's [ultravox-v0_6-qwen-3-32b](https://huggingface.co/fixie-ai/ultravox-v0_6-qwen-3-32b) achieves **2.88 WER** on librispeech (multilingual training, 32B base).

Full WER benchmarks were measured on the successor checkpoint — **[v2 reaches 2.08% LibriSpeech test-clean WER](https://huggingface.co/QuantumDesk-AI/ultravox-qwen3.6-27b-v2#benchmarks-native-inference-greedy-n100-per-set)** — and are published on its card. This base checkpoint was not separately benchmarked.

## Usage

### With vLLM (recommended for serving)

```bash
vllm serve QuantumDesk-AI/ultravox-qwen3.6-27b-base \
  --served-model-name ultravox \
  --max-model-len 32768 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --port 8000
```

### With transformers (for research)

```python
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoProcessor
import torchaudio

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(
    "QuantumDesk-AI/ultravox-qwen3.6-27b-base",
    trust_remote_code=True,
)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    "QuantumDesk-AI/ultravox-qwen3.6-27b-base",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    torch_dtype="bfloat16",
).to("cuda")

audio, sr = torchaudio.load("hello.wav")
messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "audio", "audio": audio[0].numpy(), "sampling_rate": sr},
        {"type": "text", "text": "What did I say?"},
    ]},
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(messages, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=128)
print(processor.decode(outputs[0], skip_special_tokens=True))
```

## Serving hardware

FP8 base + bf16 adapter fits on **any Blackwell (RTX PRO 6000, B200) or Hopper (H100 80/94GB)** GPU:

| Card | VRAM | Concurrent voice sessions* |
|---|---|---|
| RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell | 96 GB | ~30-40 |
| H100 94 GB | 94 GB | ~30-40 |
| B200 180 GB | 180 GB | ~80-100 |

*Compute-bound (KV cache is not the limit). Assumes ~2000 tokens context per session and voice-typical 5-6 tok/s per session sustained rate.

## Limitations

- **English only** — do not use for other languages; expect degraded quality even for accented English.
- **Clean audio only** — trained without phone-codec, noise, or music-background data. Real-world telephony will underperform relative to studio audio.
- **No chat / instruction tuning** — this is a base checkpoint. For interactive voice agents, fine-tune on your domain (see [Phase 2 discussion in repo]).
- **Reasoning under audio input** — some capacity is spent decoding audio; expect small (2-5 %) degradation vs pure-text prompting on reasoning-heavy tasks. Use text cascade for complex queries.

## License

Apache 2.0. Model weights are Quantum Desk LTD's contribution. See individual base-model licenses for [Qwen 3.6-27B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B) (Apache 2.0) and [Whisper-large-v3-turbo](https://huggingface.co/openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo) (MIT).

- [Qwen team](https://huggingface.co/Qwen) — 3.6-27B base
- [OpenAI](https://huggingface.co/openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo) — Whisper encoder

--- license: cc-by-4.0 language: - hi - te - en library_name: moshi pipeline_tag: audio-to-audio base_model: kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16 tags: - full-duplex - speech-to-speech - spoken-dialogue - moshi - hindi - telugu - indic --- # siba · full-duplex speech for Hindi, Telugu and English **siba** is a speech-to-speech dialogue model that listens and speaks at the same time, built by adapting Kyutai's [Moshi](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16) to Hindi and Telugu while keeping English. This repository holds the current **Stage 2b** checkpoint plus the Stage 1 base checkpoints it was built from. | | | |---|---| | **Model** | Moshiko (~7.7B parameters, Mimi codec) with a 48k text vocabulary (+16k Hindi/Telugu pieces) | | **Languages** | Hindi, Telugu, English | | **Training** | Stage 1: ~33k h YouTube monologue speech → Stage 2b: 517 h two-channel dialogues, 1,500 steps | | **Agent voices** | one fixed voice per language (Hindi: Ritvik) | | **Status** | research checkpoint — turn-taking works, answer relevance and response speed do not yet | | **Weights** | [`stage2b/checkpoint_001500/consolidated/consolidated.safetensors`](stage2b/checkpoint_001500/consolidated) (15.7 GB, bf16) | ## Highlights - **Listens before it speaks.** In Full-Duplex-Bench v1 it stays quiet through 78–81% of the user's mid-sentence pauses, where the original Moshi talks over every one, and it talks over the user in 25% of cases versus 89%. - **Right language, right role.** After dialogue training it replies in the language of the conversation and as an assistant; the Stage 1 model before it monologues, often in the wrong language. - **Still slow and often off-topic.** It takes 1.4–2 s to respond and often does not answer what was asked, especially in Hindi and Telugu (see [Limitations](#limitations)). ## Results ### Full-Duplex-Bench v1 (English) ![Full-Duplex-Bench v1 components, siba Stage 2b vs the original Moshiko](stage2b/assets/fdb_v1.png) | | siba Stage 2b | Moshiko | |---|:---:|:---:| | **Duplex score** (0–100) | **38.4** | **54.5** | | Talks over the user in mid-sentence pauses ↓ | **0.19 – 0.22** | 1.00 | | Talk-over share of all cases ↓ | **0.25** | 0.89 | | Takes the turn when the user finishes ↑ | 0.92 | 1.00 | | Latency to take the turn ↓ | 1.36 s | 0.00 s* | | Yields when interrupted ↑ / latency ↓ | 0.94 / 2.00 s | 0.92 / 0.68 s | | Backchannel frequency ↑ | 0.06 | 0.16 | 25% subset: the first 36 samples of each of the 5 tasks (180), both models run with the same streaming inference. The duplex score is a timing-only composite of the four components (each takes the takeover rate and gives full latency credit at ≤0.3 s, none at ≥2 s); the official GPT relevance judge was not run. \*Moshi's 0 s latency means it was already talking — its higher score partly rewards that. ### Held-out loss ![Held-out first-codebook loss by language during Stage 2b](stage2b/assets/heldout_loss.png) | Step | Hindi | Telugu | English | |---|:---:|:---:|:---:| | 0 (Stage 1, before dialogue training) | 7.94 | 7.69 | 7.71 | | 500 | 0.835 | 0.925 | 0.572 | | **1500 (released)** | **0.807** | **0.904** | **0.562** | 48 held-out one-minute units per language. No overfitting: the final step is the best. ## Quick start ```bash pip install moshi huggingface_hub ``` ```python import torch from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download from moshi.models import loaders, LMGen d = snapshot_download("BNarayanaReddy/siba", allow_patterns=["stage2b/checkpoint_001500/*", "stage2b/tokenizer.model"]) info = loaders.CheckpointInfo.from_hf_repo( "kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16", # Mimi codec moshi_weights=f"{d}/stage2b/checkpoint_001500/consolidated/consolidated.safetensors", tokenizer=f"{d}/stage2b/tokenizer.model", config_path=f"{d}/stage2b/checkpoint_001500/consolidated/config.json", ) model = info.get_moshi(device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) mimi = info.get_mimi(device="cuda"); mimi.set_num_codebooks(8) lm_gen = LMGen(model, temp=0.8, temp_text=0.7, top_k=250, top_k_text=25) # Streaming as in Moshi: Mimi-encode the user's audio one 80 ms frame (1920 samples, 24 kHz) at a time; # lm_gen.step(codes) returns the model's text token + audio codes for that frame; mimi.decode() gives its speech. ``` ## Model details
Training data — 45,204 synthetic two-channel dialogues, 517 h | Language | Train hours | Script sources | Agent voice | User voices (vary per dialogue) | |---|:---:|---|---|---| | Hindi | 211 | samvaad-hi-v1, indic-align (Wiki_Conv, OpenAssistant_T), snorbyte | Ritvik | 120 IndicVoices speakers (60 male / 60 female) | | Telugu | 178 | indic-align (Wiki_Conv, OpenAssistant_T), Updesh, snorbyte | m3_te_s38 | 120 IndicVoices speakers (60 / 60) | | English | 128 | SODA, OpenAssistant | m3_en_s0 | 100 Svarah Indian-English speakers (50 / 50) | Scripts were cleaned (prompts and reasoning stripped, replies capped at ~50 words), voiced with the Maya 3 TTS, force-aligned (MMS) and assembled into two-channel conversations: median turn gap ~0.3 s, ~25% overlapping turn changes, barge-ins where the agent yields within ~0.27 s, and backchannels from a per-voice bank. Audio is Mimi-encoded at 8 codebooks per channel; 473 dialogues (5.6 h) are held out.
Training setup — 1,500 steps on 7 × H100, 31 min | Setting | Value | |---|---| | Init | Stage 1, step 15k (`stage1/checkpoint_015000`) | | Fine-tuning | full, Mimi frozen | | Batch | 49 × 60 s (0.82 h of audio per step), ~2.4 passes over the data | | Optimizer | AdamW, LR 2e-5, one-cycle with 5% warm-up, weight decay 0.1 | | Loss | agent text + agent audio (first codebook ×100, text padding ×0.5); the user channel is input only | | Language weights | Hindi 0.35 · Telugu 0.35 · English 0.30 | Exact config: [`stage2b/args.yaml`](stage2b/args.yaml) · eval log: [`stage2b/stage_eval.jsonl`](stage2b/stage_eval.jsonl) · benchmark reports: [`stage2b/bench/`](stage2b/bench)
Stage 1 (the base) Monologue speech from YouTube — Hindi 12.8k h, Telugu 12.1k h, English 8.4k h — with the user channel silent, so it is not conversational on its own. Checkpoints are in [`stage1/`](stage1) (5k, 10k, 15k; a continuation to 30k is in progress). Stage 2b starts from step 15k.
## Limitations - **Relevance.** Replies are often fluent but not about what the user asked, most of all in Hindi and Telugu. Understanding the user's speech is weak: Stage 1 never had a user channel and Stage 2b adds only ~500 h of listening. Hindi/Telugu knowledge answers can invent facts. - **Latency.** It responds 1.4–2 s after the user finishes, against ~0.3 s gaps in its training data. - **Synthetic data only.** All voices are TTS and the timing is rule-based; no real Hindi/Telugu conversations. Long-answer sources (OpenAssistant, Updesh) give few exchanges per minute. - **Evaluation.** Benchmark numbers are English only and from a 25% subset (components can move by ±0.1). - **Audio.** Moshi's 8-codebook Mimi on top of TTS audio limits clarity. ## Repository contents
All folders | Folder | What it is | |---|---| | `stage2b/` | this model: weights, config, tokenizer, training config, eval log, benchmark reports, card images | | `stage1/` | Stage 1 checkpoints with eval logs | | `moshiko_ext16k/` | the untrained starting point: Moshiko with the text vocabulary extended 32k → 48k | | `tokenizers/` | tokenizer candidates (table below) | | `configs/`, `scripts/`, `results/` | training configs, data and training scripts, evaluation reports | **moshiko_ext16k.** Ids 0–31999 are Moshi's original pieces (weights unchanged; English tokenises to identical ids); ids 32000–47999 are Telugu/Hindi pieces whose embedding and output rows start as the mean of the byte tokens they replace. The start-of-text row moved to 48000. On original-vocab input, audio logits and the first 32,000 text logits are bit-identical to Moshiko. Apply Unicode NFC to text before tokenising. | Tokenizer | Vocab | en tokens/word | hi tokens/word | te tokens/word | |---|---|---|---|---| | original Moshi | 32,000 | 1.28 | 10.70 | 19.66 | | **extend_16k (used)** | 48,000 | 1.278 | 1.23 | 1.53 | | extend_24k | 56,000 | 1.278 | 1.19 | 1.43 | | replace_32k | 32,000 | 1.34 | 1.20 | 1.46 |
## License and attribution Weights derive from Kyutai's Moshiko (CC-BY 4.0; copyright Kyutai, modified as described above). Training scripts come from SODA (CC-BY 4.0), sarvamai/samvaad-hi-v1 (Apache-2.0), ai4bharat indic-align, microsoft/Updesh and snorbyte samples (CC-BY 4.0); user voices were cloned from AI4Bharat's IndicVoices and Svarah. Check each source's terms before uses beyond research.

# PolyPlex-14B-CJKE **A full-duplex spoken dialogue model for Chinese, Japanese, Korean and English**

Quickstart · The tokenizer · The processor · Lineage · License · Citation

> [!NOTE] > **Preview release: tokenizer and processor only.** This repository currently ships the PolyPlex text tokenizer and the > input processor. The model weights will be added to this repository when training is finished. Everything below runs > on upstream `transformers` today; no fork is needed. ## ✨ Highlights - **A vocabulary sized by speech, not by text.** Every token of a full-duplex model fills one 80 ms frame. The vocabulary was grown language by language until words stop being cut by the next word on real conversational speech, measured on Whisper word timings of YouTube speech in 110 languages. - **223,973 tokens, smaller than Gemma 3.** Helium (Moshi's vocabulary) is kept with its ids, Qwen3's tokens are merged in, and whole words and subwords are added only where speech needs them. Written-only Qwen3 words that speech never uses are dropped. - **No byte fragments in speech.** Every standard character of every language is a token, so speech never falls back to bytes, which cannot be aligned to sound. - **Drop-in for 🤗 Transformers.** `AutoTokenizer` and `AutoProcessor` load it with stock `transformers`; the processor builds the frame-aligned text, user-audio and assistant-audio streams, including the PersonaPlex persona prompt. ## 🚀 Quickstart ```bash pip install "transformers>=5.14" torch ``` ### Tokenizer ```python from transformers import AutoTokenizer tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("RetentionLabs/PolyPlex-14B-CJKE") tokenizer.tokenize("안녕하세요, 반갑습니다.") # ['▁안녕하세요', ',', '▁반갑습니다', '.'] tokenizer.tokenize("Hello there!") # ['▁Hello', '▁there', '!'] tokenizer.tokenize("你好，很高兴认识你") # ['▁', '你好', '，', '很高兴', '认识', '你'] tokenizer.tokenize("こんにちは、元気ですか") # ['▁', 'こんにちは', '、', '元', '気', 'ですか'] tokenizer.pad_token_id, tokenizer.unk_token_id # (3, 0): PAD and EPAD of the duplex text stream ``` ### Processor The processor loads the [Mimi](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/mimi) codec and turns text and audio into the three frame-aligned streams the model reads. ```python import numpy as np from transformers import AutoProcessor processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("RetentionLabs/PolyPlex-14B-CJKE", trust_remote_code=True) speech = np.zeros(24_000 * 2, dtype=np.float32) # 2 s of user speech at 24 kHz inputs = processor(text="안녕하세요", audio=speech) # input_ids (1, 25) text padded with PAD to one token per frame # user_audio_codes (1, 8, 25) Mimi codes of the user's speech # assistant_audio_codes (1, 8, 25) encoded silence, since no assistant audio was given prompt = processor(text_prompt="You are a friendly assistant who speaks Korean.") # persona prefix waveform = processor.decode_audio(inputs["user_audio_codes"]) # (1, 1, 48000) ``` ## 🔤 The tokenizer ### Why a duplex model needs its own vocabulary A text LLM can cut a rare word into many pieces: the sequence only gets longer. A full-duplex speech model writes its text stream in step with audio, **one token per 80 ms frame** (Moshi, PersonaPlex). A word must fit in the frames between its own onset and the next word's onset. When it does not, the next word overwrites its tail and the word is **cut** (Moshi, Section 3.4.4, Eq. 5). Byte fragments are worse still: a fragment of a UTF-8 character matches no sound at all. Qwen3's byte-level BPE, for example, cuts 14.5% of the tokens of spoken Korean into byte fragments, 96% of them at a word's first character. So the PolyPlex vocabulary is designed around one measurable quantity. > **Word cut rate**: the share of words whose tokens do not all survive in the text stream when the words are placed at > their real onsets, one token per frame, the way the model is trained. ### Construction | Step | What | Size | |---|---|---| | **1. Base** | Helium (Moshi's SentencePiece vocabulary) keeps every token and id. Qwen3's tokens are added with the leading space written as `▁` (`Ġword` → `▁word`); a string both have is one token, Helium's. Every string is NFC. | 32,000 + Qwen3 | | **2. Tier 1: characters** | Every standard character of each language (CLDR 48.2.3 exemplars, plus the full Unicode block for Indic, Southeast Asian and Georgian scripts), each also as a word-start form `▁c` for letters and digits. Unconditional. | 13,457 new | | **3. Tier 2: whole words** | Frequent spoken word forms that take two or more tokens, ordered by frames saved (count × (tokens − 1)), added 250 at a time while the cut rate falls. | 20,168 | | **4. Tier 3: subwords** | Subwords from a Unigram model trained on each language's multi-token spoken words, added 1,000 at a time while the cut rate falls, plus non-standard characters of the language's own scripts seen three or more times. | 64,228 | | **5. Scores** | Unigram scores by EM over the spoken text of every language, with the vocabulary fixed. | | | **6. Pruning** | Qwen3 multi-character tokens the spoken EM never uses are dropped (written Chinese and English words, symbol runs), as are unused word-start forms of single Han and kana characters. Code pieces, emoji and single characters are kept for tool use. | −30,685 | For each language, both orders are run (subwords first, then whole words; and whole words first, then subwords), and the order that reaches the target with fewer tokens is kept. A subword shortens every word that holds it, so subwords win for scripts where words take many tokens (Greek: 5,016 subwords instead of 21,016 tokens; Hindi: 6,000 instead of 19,500); whole words win where a few hundred to a few thousand forms suffice (Korean: 3,750 words). ### Measuring the cut rate - **Speech.** User-subtitled YouTube videos of [YODAS2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/espnet/yodas2) in every language that has them, Korean included. Neighbouring subtitle segments are joined into pieces of at most 25 s. - **Word timings.** Whisper large-v3, with the transcript forced (teacher forcing) and DTW over the alignment heads' cross-attention. The timings are released as [RetentionLabs/polyplex-word-timings](https://huggingface.co/datasets/RetentionLabs/polyplex-word-timings). - **Filtering.** Pieces whose alignment loss exceeds 1.61 (the 95th percentile on KsponSpeech) are subtitles that do not match the speech. Pieces where over 10% of neighbouring onsets are under 20 ms apart were not aligned. A word whose span or gap is under 30 ms per character is an alignment error: it keeps its frames but counts neither as cut nor in the total. - **Approximation.** Languages left with fewer than 2,000 timed words, and scripts without spaces, place words by their share of characters in the utterance duration (FLEURS recordings, or the script's characters per second). - **Targets.** 1%, or the lowest reachable rate (every word one token) plus 0.2 points when that is higher. The main languages, English, Korean, Japanese and Chinese, go on to the lowest rate plus 0.2 points even below 1%. ### Result Final cut rates are measured with the final tokenizer on the evaluation part of each language, held out from selection. | Language | Tier 1 | Tier 2 | Tier 3 | Word cut rate | Target | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | English | 10 | 0 | 0 | 0.18% | 0.28% | | Korean | 2,432 | 3,750 | 48 | 0.23% | 0.23% | | Japanese | 8,817 | 0 | 3 | 0.00% | 0.20% | | Chinese (Simplified) | 6,850 | 0 | 3 | 0.00% | 0.20% | | Chinese (Traditional) | 6,801 | 0 | 98 | 0.03% | 0.20% | | Cantonese | 6,801 | 0 | 0 | 0.01% | 1.00% | Across all 110 measured languages the median cut rate is 0.25%, and 109 are below their target. Punjabi stays at 1.97%: it has no subtitles in OpenSubtitles and five YODAS2 shards, so its candidate text is 2,198 lines. It is left above the target rather than filled with written text. | Vocabulary | Size | |---|---:| | Helium (Moshi, PersonaPlex) | 32,000 | | Llama 3 | 128,256 | | Qwen3 | 151,669 | | **PolyPlex** | **223,973** | | Gemma 3 | 262,144 | ### Layout and behaviour | Item | Value | |---|---| | Model | SentencePiece-style Unigram with byte fallback (`tokenizers`) | | Normalization | NFC, then spaces to `▁` with one `▁` in front of the text | | Word starts | Marked by `▁` on the first token of every word. `EPAD` marks the end of a pause and is skipped when the previous word still occupies its frame (Moshi), so it cannot mark word starts. | | Digits | One token per digit; no multi-digit tokens exist | | Ids 0 – 31,999 | Helium, unchanged: `` = 0 (`EPAD` in the duplex stream), `` = 1, `` = 2, `` = 3 (`PAD`), bytes 4 – 259 | | Ids 32,000 – 32,005 | Control tokens `` `` `` `` `` `` | | Ids 32,006 – 223,972 | The rest of the base block, then one block per script, each ordered by score | | LM head | 224,000 rows (padded to a multiple of 128). The opening frame id is 224,000 and exists only as an input row. | Control and special tokens never come out of text: their Unigram score lies far below every text piece, so a literal `` in text is cut as `▁<` `think` `>`. Data used to build the vocabulary | Use | Data | |---|---| | Standard characters | Unicode CLDR 48.2.3 exemplar characters | | Candidate words and EM scores | OpenSubtitles (first 200,000 lines per language), YODAS2 subtitles of shards not used for evaluation, FLEURS transcripts, Korean spoken corpora (AI Hub daily multi-session dialogue, colloquial Korean–English), Wikipedia only for languages without spoken text | | Word cut rate | YODAS2 pieces with Whisper word timings; FLEURS read speech as a reference only | | Check of the method on Korean | KsponSpeech evaluation split |
## 🎛 The processor `processing_polyplex.py` depends on upstream `transformers` only. Its behaviour matches the PersonaPlex processor output for output (tested on text, audio, assistant audio and persona prompts). | Input | Output | |---|---| | `text` | `input_ids`, `attention_mask`, padded with `PAD` to one token per audio frame | | `audio` | `user_audio_codes` `(batch, 8, frames)` | | `assistant_audio` | `assistant_audio_codes` `(batch, 8, frames)` | | A stream left out | Filled with Mimi-encoded silence, not with a reserved id | | `voice_prompt`, `text_prompt` | The persona prefix in front of the inputs (needs `pyloudnorm` for the voice prompt) | The persona prefix follows PersonaPlex's training format: | Stage | Text | Assistant stream | User stream | |---|---|---|---| | Voice prompt | `PAD` | the voice sample | 440 Hz tone | | 0.5 s | `PAD` | silence | tone | | Text prompt | ` … `, one token per frame | silence | tone | | 0.5 s | `PAD` | silence | tone | ## 🧬 Lineage ``` kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16 ──▶ nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1 ──┐ ├──▶ RetentionLabs/PolyPlex-14B-CJKE Qwen/Qwen3-8B ──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` PolyPlex keeps PersonaPlex's attention, its feed-forward layers, its depth decoder and the Mimi codec, and places the feed-forward layers of Qwen3-8B beside PersonaPlex's in every layer. Qwen3 carries multilingual knowledge; PersonaPlex's feed-forward layers keep the duplex behaviour of speaking, listening and turn-taking. The text vocabulary joins Helium's and Qwen3's as described above. ## 📚 Related work | Work | What PolyPlex takes from it | |---|---| | [Moshi](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00037) (Kyutai, 2024) | The full-duplex architecture, the frame-aligned text stream with `PAD`/`EPAD` (Section 3.4.4), the Helium vocabulary and the Mimi codec | | [PersonaPlex](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06053) (NVIDIA, 2026) | The duplex checkpoint PolyPlex is grafted onto, and the persona prompt the processor builds | | [J-Moshi](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02979) (Ohashi et al., Interspeech 2025) | A Japanese Moshi, pre-trained on large-scale Japanese spoken dialogue (J-CHAT) and fine-tuned on 344 hours of stereo dialogue | | [Human-1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23295) (Josh Talks, 2026) | A Hindi Moshi with a Hindi tokenizer and re-initialized text parameters, trained on 26,000 hours of real telephone conversations | | [Qwen3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09388) (Qwen Team, 2025) | The multilingual feed-forward layers and token strings | | [Pretraining LLMs with NVFP4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25149) (NVIDIA, 2025) | Which parts stay in high precision when the backbone runs in NVFP4: embeddings, the LM head, normalizations and attention, and a share of the linear layers | | [An Empirical Study of Qwen3 Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02214) (2025) | Qwen3 holds up under 4-bit weights but collapses when activations are quantized to 4-bit integers, which is why the backbone uses block-scaled NVFP4 and is checked layer by layer | J-Moshi and Human-1 adapt Moshi to one new language each with thousands of hours of that language's conversational speech. PolyPlex takes multilingual knowledge from a text LLM instead, so a new language needs its text and a little speech rather than a large conversational corpus. ## 📜 License This repository is governed by the [**NVIDIA Open Model License Agreement**](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/agreements/enterprise-software/nvidia-open-model-license/), because PolyPlex is derived from [PersonaPlex](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1). The first 32,000 tokens of the vocabulary are Moshi's Helium tokenizer. - Token strings and, in the full model, feed-forward weights come from [Qwen3-8B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B) by the Qwen team, released under [Apache-2.0](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B/blob/main/LICENSE). - `processing_polyplex.py` is released under Apache-2.0. ## 📖 Citation ```bibtex @misc{polyplex2026, title = {PolyPlex: Data-efficient Multilingual Transfer for Duplex Spoken LMs}, author = {{RetentionLabs}}, year = {2026}, howpublished = {\url{https://huggingface.co/RetentionLabs/PolyPlex-14B-CJKE}} } @article{defossez2024moshi, title = {Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue}, author = {D{\'e}fossez, Alexandre and Mazar{\'e}, Laurent and Orsini, Manu and Royer, Am{\'e}lie and P{\'e}rez, Patrick and J{\'e}gou, Herv{\'e} and Grave, Edouard and Zeghidour, Neil}, journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.00037}, year = {2024} } @article{roy2026personaplex, title = {PersonaPlex: Voice and Role Control for Full Duplex Conversational Speech Models}, author = {Roy, Rajarshi and Raiman, Jonathan and Lee, Sang-gil and Ene, Teodor-Dumitru and Kirby, Robert and Kim, Sungwon and Kim, Jaehyeon and Catanzaro, Bryan}, journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2602.06053}, year = {2026} } @article{qwen3technicalreport, title = {Qwen3 Technical Report}, author = {{Qwen Team}}, journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.09388}, year = {2025} } ```

[![GitHub](./assets/badges/github-badge.svg)](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Audio8_TTS) [![License](./assets/badges/license-badge.svg)](./LICENSE) [![Demo](./assets/badges/demo-badge.svg)](https://edge0-ai.github.io/Audio8_TTS/realistic-0.6b/) [![arXiv](./assets/badges/arxiv-badge.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14776) [![Playground](./assets/badges/playground-badge.svg)](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b) [Languages](#supported-languages) · [Quick start](#installation) · [Serving](#high-throughput-serving-sglang-omni) · [Evaluation](#evaluation)
--- **Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6B** builds on [Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b), delivering **substantially improved speech realism** while retaining its compact **0.6B** architecture and zero-shot voice cloning capabilities. This release supports **23 languages**, adding **12 languages compared with Preview**. It uses the same Transformers inference interface as Preview. This repository includes the complete model checkpoint, its 44.1 kHz neural audio codec, tokenizer, processor, and custom Transformers code. Try speech generation and voice cloning in the [interactive Playground](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b). Hosted on Hugging Face ZeroGPU; availability depends on the queue and your daily GPU allowance. Audio8 is also participating in [TTS Arena](https://tts-agi-tts-arena-v2.hf.space/), where it has received encouraging ratings from listeners. We are grateful to everyone who has listened and voted. ## Highlights - **Improved realism:** more natural prosody and expressive delivery, building on Preview. - **Broader multilingual coverage:** 23 languages, including 12 additions to Preview's 11 supported languages. - **Compact model:** 601 million main-model parameters, with the audio codec bundled separately. - **Flexible generation:** zero-shot voice cloning from a reference recording and transcript, or speech generation without a reference. - **GPU serving:** an SGLang Omni adapter with paged attention, dynamic batching, and an OpenAI-compatible speech API. ## Supported Languages | Coverage | Languages | |---|---| | Supported in Preview (11) | Cantonese, Chinese, Dutch, English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Spanish | | Added in Realistic (12) | Arabic, Finnish, Hindi, Indonesian, Malay, Norwegian, Portuguese, Russian, Swedish, Thai, Turkish, Vietnamese | > **Note:** Language quality varies; see the per-language evaluation below. Benchmark coverage includes some additional languages and is distinct from the supported-language list. ## Model Details Audio8 TTS uses a DualAR architecture inspired by [Fish Audio S2 Pro](https://github.com/fishaudio/fish-speech). The slow AR transformer predicts one semantic token for each audio frame. The fast AR transformer predicts the frame's codec codebooks, conditioned on the slow hidden state and preceding codebooks. | Component | Configuration | |---|---| | Main model | 601,159,424 parameters, excluding the codec | | Slow AR | 24 layers, width 896, 14 attention heads, 2 KV heads | | Fast AR | 4 layers, width 896, 14 attention heads, 2 KV heads | | Acoustic tokens | 10 codebooks, 4,096 entries per codebook | | Codec | 44.1 kHz, 2,048 samples per model frame (~21.5 frames/s) | | Context | Up to 2,048 packed text/audio positions | The bundled codec handles both reference-audio encoding and waveform decoding, so no additional codec checkpoint is required. The **0.6B** size refers to the main DualAR model; the codec is excluded from that parameter count. --- ## Installation Python 3.10 or newer and a CUDA-capable GPU are recommended. ```bash pip install "torch>=2.5.0" "torchaudio>=2.5.0" \ "transformers>=4.57.0,<5" "soundfile>=0.12" "safetensors>=0.4" ``` The Transformers release package was smoke-tested with PyTorch 2.8.0 and Transformers 4.57.3 on an NVIDIA H20 using BF16. Checks covered model loading, English and Chinese generation with and without reference audio, and generation in Arabic, Cantonese, Portuguese, and Russian. These are runtime checks, separate from the benchmark results below. ## Usage The model uses custom Transformers code. Review the files in this repository, then load it with `trust_remote_code=True`. ### Zero-shot voice cloning Use a clean reference recording. Its transcript must match the spoken content exactly. ```python import soundfile as sf import torch from transformers import AutoModel, AutoProcessor model_id = "Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True) model = AutoModel.from_pretrained( model_id, trust_remote_code=True, dtype=dtype, ).eval().to(device) inputs = processor( text=["Welcome to Audio8 TTS. It is wonderful to hear from you."], reference_audio=["reference.wav"], reference_text=["The exact transcript of the reference recording."], return_tensors="pt", ) inputs = {name: value.to(device) for name, value in inputs.items()} with torch.inference_mode(): output = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=1024, temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95, top_k=50, do_sample=True, return_dict_in_generate=True, ) waveforms, waveform_lengths = model.decode_audio(output.codes) audio = waveforms[0, : int(waveform_lengths[0])].float().cpu().numpy() sf.write("output.wav", audio, model.config.codec_sample_rate) ``` ### Generation without a reference Replace the processor call above with: ```python inputs = processor( text=["This utterance does not use a reference voice."], return_tensors="pt", ) ``` Then move the inputs to the model device and run the same generation and decoding steps. For command-line inference, batching, and supervised fine-tuning, see the [Audio8 TTS repository](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Audio8_TTS), using `Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b` as the model path. ## High-throughput serving: SGLang Omni The [SGLang Omni adapter](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Audio8_TTS/tree/master/sglang_omni) provides GPU serving for Audio8 TTS. It is installed as an independent model plugin and does not overwrite SGLang Omni core files. | Capability | Support | |---|---| | Attention and batching | SGLang paged attention and dynamic batching | | DualAR execution | Slow AR serving with a fixed KV cache for the Fast AR codebook decoder | | Voice cloning | Reference-audio encoding and waveform decoding | | API | OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/speech` service | Use the **0.6B** configuration, `sglang_omni/configs/audio8_tts_0_6b.yaml`, and set the model path to `Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b` or its downloaded snapshot. The adapter supports generation without a reference and zero-shot voice cloning. See the [deployment guide](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Audio8_TTS#sglang-omni-serving) for compatible dependency versions, installation, server configuration, and API examples. > **Validation note:** Audio8-TTS-Realistic was tested on an NVIDIA H20 in BF16 for generation with and without a reference through the non-streaming speech API, with Torch compilation and CUDA graphs disabled. These checks validate runtime compatibility; throughput and streaming were not benchmarked. --- ## Evaluation Error rates are percentages (**lower is better**). Speaker similarity (SIM) is on a **0–1 scale** (**higher is better**). These metrics measure intelligibility and speaker similarity; they do not directly measure perceived speech realism. ### Benchmark summary **Audio8-TTS-Preview** and **Audio8-TTS-Realistic**, both **0.6B**: | Benchmark | Coverage | Preview error % ↓ | Realistic error % ↓ | Preview SIM ↑ | Realistic SIM ↑ | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Seed-TTS | English / Chinese | 1.23 | 1.25 | 0.682 | 0.704 | | CV3 | 8 shared languages | 4.80 | 4.56 | — | 0.663 | | CV3 | 9 core languages | — | 4.86 | — | 0.661 | | MiniMax | 24 evaluated languages | — | 5.89 | — | 0.754 | > **Note:** Values are unweighted language macro averages. Preview results are calculated from its [published model card](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b#evaluation), with SIM converted from percentages to a 0–1 scale. The two releases were evaluated separately. A dash means the corresponding result was not reported on Preview's card. > > Seed-TTS averages English WER and Chinese CER, excluding hard Chinese. The shared CV3 subset is Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean, German, French, Spanish, and Italian; the 9-language set also includes Russian. CV3 averages exclude hard subsets and the 13 additional languages. MiniMax averages all 24 evaluated languages, including languages outside the supported list. ### Reference comparison The following error rates come from the sources used in our technical report. Different evaluation pipelines and text normalization make this a reference comparison rather than a strictly matched ranking. A dash means that a result is unavailable in the comparison, not that the model lacks support. | Model | Parameters (B) | Seed-TTS EN/ZH error ↓ | CV3 (9) error ↓ | MiniMax (24) error ↓ | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | **Audio8-TTS-Realistic** | **0.6** | **1.25** | **4.86** | **5.89** | | Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B | 0.6 | 1.12 | — | — | | Qwen3-TTS-1.7B | 1.7 | 1.01 | 7.73 | 27.41 | | Higgs Audio v3 | 4 | 1.11 | 4.41 | 2.74 | | Higgs Audio v2 | 4.7 | 1.17 | 4.49 | — | | Fish S2 Pro | 4.6 | 1.32 | 4.49 | 4.40 | | MOSS-TTS-v1.5 | 8.5 | 1.52 | 6.11 | 3.78 | | CosyVoice3-1.5B | 1.5 | 1.67 | 6.89 | — | | VoxCPM2 | 2.3 | 1.41 | 5.35 | — | > **Sources:** Qwen Seed-TTS results are from the Qwen3-TTS report, linked from the [official Qwen3-TTS repository](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-TTS); Qwen's CV3/MiniMax results, all Higgs Audio v3 results, and MOSS-TTS-v1.5's CV3/MiniMax results are from [Boson AI's evaluation](https://huggingface.co/bosonai/higgs-audio-v3-tts-4b). Fish S2 Pro's MiniMax result is from the Fish Audio S2 report, linked from the [official Fish Speech repository](https://github.com/fishaudio/fish-speech); its Seed-TTS/CV3 results and Higgs Audio v2's results are our reevaluations. MOSS-TTS-v1.5's Seed-TTS result and the CosyVoice3/VoxCPM2 results are compiled in the [VoxCPM repository](https://github.com/OpenBMB/VoxCPM). It turns speech into two streams of integer tokens and decodes them back to 24 kHz audio. It was trained mostly on English and 10 Indian languages, and it is strongest on Indian languages: among codecs at about 1 kbps, it keeps the most words in every one of the 10 we tested. ## Key features - **Low bitrate:** 1.09 kbps, 75 tokens per second. - **Two token streams:** a content stream (25 Hz) that carries the words, and an acoustic stream (50 Hz) that carries the voice and detail. - **Split FSQ, not RVQ:** each stream is a single FSQ grid. Content is coded first, and one acoustic grid codes what remains, instead of a stack of residual codebooks. Each frame is one id per stream, with no learned codebook. - **16 kHz in, 24 kHz out:** any input sample rate is resampled to 16 kHz. - **One file:** all weights are in `model.safetensors`. Nothing else is downloaded. - **Commercial use allowed:** Apache 2.0. All training data is under open licences, none of them non-commercial. ## Model details | | | |---|---| | Content stream | 25 Hz, FSQ 8 × 3 levels = 6,561 ids, 317 bps | | Acoustic stream | 50 Hz, FSQ 6 × 6 levels = 46,656 ids, 775 bps | | Bitrate | 1.09 kbps | | Parameters | 624 M in the file, 387 M of them w2v-BERT 2.0; decoding alone uses 186 M | | Licence | Apache 2.0 | The content stream quantises w2v-BERT 2.0 features (layer 16). The acoustic stream quantises what a CNN encoder hears beyond the content stream. A transformer decoder with an iSTFT head turns the sum back into audio. # OmniVoice on Apple Neural Engine

Core AI conversion of [k2-fsa/OmniVoice](https://huggingface.co/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) for multilingual speech synthesis, voice cloning, and voice design, using [tinkerbox-ane](https://github.com/WeGoToMars/tinkerbox).

The FP16 Qwen3 diffusion transformer and audio projection run fully on the ANE. The 24 kHz acoustic codec decoder also runs fully on the ANE. Text processing, embeddings, scheduling, sampling, codec lookup/projection and reference encoding run on the CPU while your GPU stays idle and cool 😎❄️.

Requires macOS 27, Apple Silicon M4 or newer, and Python 3.12 or 3.13. M1 and M2 are not supported: their ANE compiler rejects the long-context attention. M3 is not supported because the codec exceeds its ANE tensor-width limit.

## Usage

Install `tinkerbox-ane[speech]>=2.2.0`. The downloader fetches only this Mac's bundle: its `checkpoint` folder carries the tokenizer, configuration, embeddings, and audio codec the CPU uses.

Generate speech and save it as WAV:

```python
import soundfile as sf
from tinkerbox_ane import omnivoice
from tinkerbox_ane.bundle import download_bundle

bundle = download_bundle("omnivoice", "wegotomars/OmniVoice-CoreAI-ANE", "v2.2.0")
with omnivoice.load(bundle) as model:
    audio = model.generate("Hello! Welcome to Tinkerbox.", language="en", seed=42)[0]
    sf.write("speech.wav", audio, model.sampling_rate)
```

Clone a voice from a recording and its transcript, reusing the downloaded bundle:

```python
with omnivoice.load(bundle) as model:
    voice = model.create_voice_clone_prompt(
        "reference.m4a", ref_text="The words spoken in the reference recording."
    )
    audio = model.generate("A new sentence in the same voice.", voice_clone_prompt=voice, seed=42)[0]
    sf.write("cloned.wav", audio, model.sampling_rate)
```

For voice design, pass an instruction such as `instruct="female, low pitch, British accent"` to `generate`. Voice prompts can be saved with `voice.save("voice.pt")` and reused with `model.load_voice_clone_prompt("voice.pt")`.

Text, reference, and generated audio share the original model's full 40,960-position context per diffusion call. Up to 4,096 positions run as one fused ANE call, longer sequences use blockwise attention. Long-form speech uses upstream chunking above its default 30-second threshold. OmniVoice refines every audio frame together until the last diffusion step, so it does not stream partial audio.

## Supported architectures

| --- | --- |
| `h16g` | Apple M4 |
| `h16s` | Apple M4 Pro |
| `h16c` | Apple M4 Max |
| `h17g` | Apple M5 |
| `h17s` | Apple M5 Pro |
| `h17c` | Apple M5 Max |
| `h17d` | Apple M5 Ultra |

## Benchmarks

These measurements predate the ANE codec decoder update and describe the previous CPU-codec bundles.

Measured October 26, 2026 on Apple M5 Pro (`h17s`, 24 GiB), macOS 27.0.1, warm. Real-time multiplier is audio duration divided by generation time (higher is faster); RTF is its inverse (lower is faster).

| Request | Audio | Generation time | Real-time multiplier | RTF | ANE energy |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Automatic voice | 4.4 s | 1.11 s | 4.0× | 0.25 | 4.2 J |
| Saved clone | 2.9 s | 1.03 s | 2.8× | 0.35 | 3.8 J |
| Passage, default chunking | 18.5 s | 5.74 s | 3.2× | 0.31 | 21.2 J |

| Memory | Peak |
| --- | ---: |
| Wired, including ANE weights | 1.35 GiB |

## Accuracy

The updated ANE-codec bundle passed public speech regressions on M5 Pro (`h17s`), macOS 27.0.1, on October 29, 2026: automatic voice, design, cloning, ordered batches, seed replay, request isolation, transcription and offline bundled-checkpoint loading. Other advertised chips are cross-compiled with full ANE placement verification; on-device correctness and performance are established only on M5 Pro.

Compared with the original `omnivoice==0.2.1` in CPU FP16 on identical inputs:

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Full-transformer logits (96–3,000 positions), cosine | ≥ 0.999985 |
| 40,960-key attention kernel, cosine | ≥ 0.999998 |
| 60-second passage, mean transcription error | 0.187 (original 0.193) |

# Audio-R1 — Qwen2.5-Omni-7B (LoRA)

LoRA adapter for [Qwen/Qwen2.5-Omni-7B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Omni-7B) trained with **Audio-R1**, an RL post-training framework that uses audio self-supervised tasks as a source of verifiable rewards.

- **Paper:** [Audio-R1: Audio Reasoning through Reinforcement Learning on Self-Supervised Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34609)
- **Project page:** https://ijihoon98.github.io/Audio-R1/

## Training Details

| Hyperparameter | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Method | GRPO, 1 epoch, LoRA |
| Reward | accuracy (1.0 if the chosen letter is correct) + format (0.2) |
| Format reward | `<think>` and `<answer>` tags present |
| Optimizer / LR schedule | AdamW, cosine |
| Learning rate / warmup ratio | 5e-6 / 0.03 |
| Rollouts per prompt | 8 |
| Sampling temperature / top-p | 0.8 / 0.9 |
| KL coefficient β | 0.04 |
| Clip ε | 0.2 |
| Per-device batch × grad. accumulation | 8 × 4 |
| GPUs | 4 |
| LoRA rank / α / dropout | 8 / 32 / 0.05 |
| LoRA targets | all linear layers; audio encoder frozen |
| Precision / seed | bf16 / 42 |

## Usage

```python
import torch
from peft import PeftModel
from transformers import Qwen2_5OmniForConditionalGeneration, Qwen2_5OmniProcessor
from qwen_omni_utils import process_mm_info

base = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-Omni-7B"
processor = Qwen2_5OmniProcessor.from_pretrained(base)
model = Qwen2_5OmniForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(base, torch_dtype=torch.float16, device_map="auto")
model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(model, "NearAndDear98/Audio-R1-Qwen2.5-Omni-7B").eval()

SYSTEM = (
    "Your response MUST contain two parts in this exact order: "
    "1. Your reasoning enclosed within <think> </think> tags. "
    "2. The final answer — a single letter for the correct option — enclosed "
    "within <answer> </answer> tags."
)
conversation = [
    {"role": "system", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": SYSTEM}]},
    {"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "audio", "audio": "example.wav"},
        {"type": "text", "text": "Question ...\n(A) ...\n(B) ...\n(C) ...\n(D) ..."},
    ]},
]
text = processor.apply_chat_template(conversation, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False)
audios, images, videos = process_mm_info(conversation, use_audio_in_video=False)
inputs = processor(text=text, audio=audios, images=images, videos=videos,
                   return_tensors="pt", padding=True, use_audio_in_video=False).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024, thinker_do_sample=False,
                     use_audio_in_video=False, return_audio=False)
print(processor.batch_decode(out, skip_special_tokens=True)[0])
```
